the others are subtracted as traced before the trail pass, and a seed on one is kept only if the better model fits it to χ²/dof ≤ 1.5 Seeds along a satellite near the trail's direction made false stars; stars it crosses are kept crates/fayde-detect/src/trail.rs (star_like, run) A seed is also fitted as a point when 40% of its light along the line lies within two widths of its brightest point, or its trail fit has χ²/dof > 2 The tracked object and other point-like sources, at a fraction of the cost of fitting every seed twice crates/fayde-detect/src/trail.rs (POINT_CHECK_*) p_star = (1 − local false discovery rate of the filtered peak) × the trail model's posterior against a point (equal priors); positions known no better than half a trail along or two widths across are dropped; a fit counts when its last steps are under half their errors (steps that reverse are halved) As the point pass for the first factor; the rest from synthetic and real frames, where faint long trails and trails cut by the edge wander along the trail crates/fayde-detect/src/trail.rs (run, fit) The solver's isotropic position error is the larger of the errors along and across the trail Conservative: the solver takes one isotropic error per source crates/fayde-detect/src/lib.rs (trails) The census and the trail pass run at full resolution when the point pass binned; the point pass's hot pixels and cosmic-ray tracks are trusted only when it ran at full resolution, else artifacts are found by their pixels alone Trails read as wide stars make the point pass bin, and binned it calls pieces of trails sharp crates/fayde-detect/src/lib.rs (detect, trails) exp(−t²/2) and erf(t) from tables 1/512 apart, linear between entries Fayde's own; the tables are built with fayde_core::Portable, so the same on every machine crates/fayde-detect/src/trail.rs (tables)

docs.title: Considered and not adopted
docs.text: Algorithm Source Why not A pattern-hash stage ahead of the pair seeds when a pointing, a tight scale and an index are all given Fayde's own Measured on 146 real source lists of 4 to 60 sources with the two all-sky indexes. The hash stage solved 123 of the 134 solvable lists and halved the median (1.3 ms against 2.8 ms), but a stage that finds nothing costs 37 to 395 ms in a 17 GB table (1 ms in a regional one, which is what first suggested the idea), and a match that comes late costs up to 86 ms: mean 24.0 ms against 4.5 ms with the pair seeds first. A cap on the stage gains under 10%. Pair seeds solved every list the hash did Radon-transform streak search (fast Radon transform; median Radon) Nir, Zackay & Ofek 2018, AJ 156, 229; Stark et al. 2022, ACS ISR 2022-08 Finds long streaks below the per-pixel noise, at about 0.9 to 10 s per megapixel after stars are removed. Fayde needs streaks kept out of the star list, which only streaks above the threshold threaten. Hough transform on thresholded pixels (kernel-based: Fernandes & Oliveira 2008; Rubin maskStreaks) Pattern Recognition 41, 299; DMTN-197 Each ridge-like peak already carries its direction, so a trace from it replaces the vote. A-contrario alignment of points Lezama et al. 2015, IEEE TPAMI 37(3), 499 For grouping fragments of a faint streak; the tracer follows the pixels instead. Its significance test would suit a fragment-only detector. Exact null distribution of peak heights with Benjamini–Hochberg selection (STEM) Schwartzman, Gavrilov & Adler 2011, Ann. Stat. 39, 3290; Cheng & Schwartzman 2017 The continuous-field formula is 25 to 35% conservative for a kernel of about 1 px (Lin, Schwartzman & Davenport 2025, arXiv:2501.13239); the pixel bound is tighter there and is used with it. Iterative Gaussian-windowed centroid Bertin & Arnouts 1996 (SExtractor XWIN) Equal accuracy on the matched-filtered peak at a fraction of the cost. 4-D quad codes searched in a kd-tree Lang et al. 2010 Fayde's 5 sorted edge ratios describe the same four-point shape as a quad code, and the hash lookup already enumerates neighboring bins and re-checks the exact shape, which is the continuous-tolerance behavior a kd-tree gives. What astrometry.net adds for blind solving is its scale-band index series, which Fayde adopts.

docs.title: Source list format
docs.text:
A source list contains the positions of sources that you detect in one image. Use a source list when you detect the stars yourself. When you give Fayde the image with --image, you don't need a source list.

Fayde reads a source list with the --sources option of fayde solve, fayde verify, and fayde refit. The fayde detect command writes one with -o.

docs.title: File structure
docs.text:
A source list is a FITS file with a binary table extension. Each row of the table describes one source. Fayde reads the first binary table that has X and Y columns and ignores columns that this page doesn't list. Fayde recognizes a source list by this table, not by the filename.

Name a source list after its image, with the suffix .sources.fits. For example, use frame.sources.fits for the source list from frame.fits.

The fayde detect command sets the table's EXTNAME keyword to SOURCES and records the Fayde version in the CREATOR keyword. Fayde doesn't require these keywords in a source list that you write yourself.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
The following table lists the columns that Fayde reads:

Column Required Content X Yes The horizontal position of the source, in pixels Y Yes The vertical position of the source, in pixels FLUX No The integrated flux, in any linear unit. Fayde uses it to order the sources by brightness SIGMA or SIGMA_PX No The 1σ centroid error, in pixels. Fayde ignores a value that isn't positive P_STAR No The prior probability that the source is a real star, from 0 to 1. Fayde ignores a value outside that range TRUNCATED No Whether the frame edge or a mask cuts the source. A logical or integer column, where a nonzero value means true

Positions follow the FITS pixel convention: the center of the first pixel is at (1, 1), and X increases along a row of the image.

When a source has no SIGMA value, Fayde uses the value of --pixel-error, which is 1 pixel by default.

docs.title: Image size
docs.text: Fayde needs the width and height of the image. In the table header or the primary header, set the IMAGEW and IMAGEH keywords to the dimensions in pixels. If the source list doesn't have these keywords, Fayde takes the size from the frame header (--header) or from the --width and --height options.

docs.title: Trail keywords
docs.text:
When every star in the image is a trail of one length and direction, a source list can record the trail with two keywords in the table header:

Keyword Content TRAILLEN The full length of the trail, in pixels TRAILANG The direction of the trail, in degrees from +x toward +y

The fayde detect command writes both keywords when it measures the stars as trails. When you pass a source list that has both keywords with --sources, Fayde gives that trail to the solver, unless you give --trail-length and --trail-angle. If one of the keywords is missing, Fayde ignores the other.

docs.title: Write a source list
docs.text:
In this example, x, y, and flux are sequences with one value for each source, and the image is 4,096 by 4,096 pixels. The x and y positions must be 1-based. If your detector gives 0-based positions, add 1 to each position. To write and solve a source list, follow these steps:

  1. In Python, with the astropy package installed, write the source list with an Astropy table:
from astropy.table import Table

table = Table({"X": x, "Y": y, "FLUX": flux})
table.meta["IMAGEW"] = 4096
table.meta["IMAGEH"] = 4096
table.write("frame.sources.fits", format="fits")
  1. In a terminal, solve the source list with --sources:
fayde solve --sources frame.sources.fits --header FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o OUTPUT

Replace the following:

  • FRAME: The path to the FITS image
  • UCAC4_DIR: The path to the directory that contains u4b
  • OUTPUT: The path to the WCS file to write

For more information about solving a frame, see Solve a frame.

docs.title: Use the command line
docs.text: To install the fayde command, see Install Fayde. To download the catalog for solving, see Get the UCAC4 catalog.

docs.title: Solve a frame
docs.text:
To solve an image with the local catalog and check the result, follow these steps:

  1. In a terminal, pass the FITS image and the catalog to fayde solve:
fayde solve --image FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o OUTPUT

Replace the following:

  • FRAME: The path to the FITS image, for example frame.fits
  • UCAC4_DIR: The path to the directory that contains u4b
  • OUTPUT: The path to the WCS file to write, for example frame.wcs

The directory of OUTPUT must exist, and OUTPUT can't be one of the input files. If a path contains spaces, enclose it in quotation marks.

Fayde finds the stars in the image and reads the pointing, pixel scale, observation time, and image size from its header. Fayde then prints a JSON report to standard output.

  1. Check the report's solved field:

  2. When solved is true, Fayde writes the solution to OUTPUT as FITS WCS header cards.

  3. When solved is false, Fayde writes no solution, and the report's reason field says why.

Fayde returns an exit status of 0 when the run completes, with or without a solution. If the run fails, Fayde returns an exit status of 1 and prints the error to standard error. If the solver fails after Fayde reads the inputs, for example because a zone file that the solve needs is missing, Fayde also prints a JSON report to standard output. That report has error set to true and the error in reason.

For more information about the report fields, see Read the report.

When a run writes no solution, Fayde removes any file that already exists at OUTPUT. Fayde keeps the file if it rejects the command before the run starts, if its initial check finds that it can't write to OUTPUT, or if OUTPUT is one of the input files.

docs.title: Set the catalog directory once
docs.text:
To leave out --ucac4, set the FAYDE_UCAC4 environment variable to the path to the catalog directory. Each fayde command that has a --ucac4 option uses the variable when you leave out the option. A --ucac4 option on the command line takes precedence. In Python, fayde.Solver() without a catalog directory also uses the variable.

On Linux or macOS, set the variable for the current terminal session:

export FAYDE_UCAC4="UCAC4_DIR"

On Windows, set the variable for the current PowerShell session:

$env:FAYDE_UCAC4 = "UCAC4_DIR"

Replace UCAC4_DIR with the path to the directory that contains u4b.

docs.title: Use your own source list
docs.text:
If you detect the stars yourself, pass a source list with --sources in place of the image. A source list is a FITS binary table with X and Y columns. For the columns that Fayde reads, see the source list format.

To solve a source list, pass it together with the FITS file that has the frame's header:

fayde solve --sources SOURCES --header FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o OUTPUT

Replace SOURCES with the path to the source list, for example frame.sources.fits. Fayde uses only the header from the file at FRAME.

docs.title: Detect stars without solving
docs.text:
To find the stars in an image and write them as a source list, use fayde detect:

fayde detect --image FRAME -o SOURCES

Fayde prints a JSON report with the background, the noise, the width of the stars, and every source that it found. The report also lists the streaks that cross the image, such as satellite streaks, and the hot pixels and cosmic-ray hits that Fayde set aside. With -o, Fayde also writes the sources to SOURCES, in the format that --sources reads. For more information about the report fields, see Read the detection report.

When Fayde measures stars as points and their full width at half maximum (FWHM) is about 1 pixel or less at full resolution, it keeps sources that are too sharp for the usual shape checks. A star this narrow can put nearly all its light in one pixel, so the source list can also include hot pixels and compact cosmic-ray hits.

If your instrument profile has a charge_transfer field, add --instrument PROFILE so that the report and SOURCES hold corrected positions. For more information, see Correct charge-transfer smear.

To list the detection options and their default values, run fayde detect --help. The same options work with fayde solve --image. The --detect-threshold option sets the peak threshold in σ of the filtered image, and its value must be at least 1.5.

If background subtraction clipped many sky pixels to the same minimum value, such as zero, Fayde accounts for the clipping when estimating the background and setting detection thresholds. The clipped-sky model requires floor pixels mixed with sky noise across most of the image's sky tiles. Frames with a constant border and ordinary sky use the standard background estimate.

Tracking a satellite, slewing, or rolling a camera can smear every star during an exposure. Fayde checks each image for this motion and reports its decision in mode, which has one of the following values:

  • points: The stars are points, or trails too short to measure as trails.
  • trails: Every star is a straight trail of the same length and direction. The trail field gives the length and direction, and each source has a position error along the trail (sigma_along_px) and across it (sigma_across_px). Point-like sources, such as the tracked object, have the class point and aren't used to solve the frame.
  • kernel: Fayde measures the stars with a template learned from the image. A shared curved path uses one template. Field rotation uses templates that vary with position in the image. Each reported position is the center of the star's light over the exposure.
  • refused: Fayde finds evidence of trails but can't establish a consistent model, so it measures the stars as points. The census field gives the reason.

To measure every star as a point, add --no-trails to fayde detect or fayde solve.

If an image measured in trails or kernel mode gives no solution before the time and hypothesis limits are reached, fayde solve retries with point detections. The retried_as_points field records the retry outcome in solved and the original census in trails_census. If the retry fails to read the catalog, the report carries the error and its reason, plus the first attempt's search trace and hypothesis count.

The fayde solve --image command passes a measured trail to the solver. With -o, fayde detect records the measured trail in the source list, and fayde solve --sources passes that trail to the solver. For more information about the keywords that hold the trail, see Trail keywords.

If an image shows star trails in more than one direction, give the expected direction with --trail-angle, in degrees from +x toward +y. Fayde uses the angle to choose a direction and measures the trail from the image. The fayde detect command accepts --trail-angle alone. It reports an error if you give --trail-length without --trail-angle.

With fayde solve, fayde verify, or fayde refit, give --trail-length in pixels and --trail-angle together, or neither. With --image, the angle also guides detection. The two values replace the measured or recorded trail in the solve.

docs.title: Detect streaks without a catalog
docs.text:
To find streaks in an image and save the detection report to a file, use fayde detect:

fayde detect --image frame.fits > frame.detections.json

Read the JSON report's streaks array for straight streak candidates, longest first. This command works without a star catalog or WCS. The optional -o FITS output contains the stars used for solving, so read streak measurements from the JSON report.

Each candidate has these fields.

Fields Meaning x0, y0, x1, y1 Estimated visible endpoints in FITS 1-based pixel coordinates length_px, angle_deg Visible length in pixels and line orientation from +x toward +y, modulo 180° width_sigma_px, flux Cross-streak Gaussian width in pixels and integrated signal above the background photometry_masked A recognized crossing star was masked. Flux estimates the missing samples at the median ridge height. SNR uses the unmasked samples only. snr, coverage Integrated signal-to-noise ratio of the unmasked ridge and fraction of the visible length above the tracing threshold touches_edge, cosmic_ray An endpoint reaches the image edge, or the candidate is narrow enough to be flagged as a possible detector track, respectively

The tracer starts from a detectable elongated peak, so it can miss a faint streak that becomes visible only when integrated along its length. In trailed-star frames, Fayde uses the shared stellar trails as astrometric sources and reports the remaining streak candidates in streaks. Treat cosmic_ray as a shape flag and the endpoint order as a geometric convention. Object identity and direction of motion require other evidence.

docs.title: Specify the pointing and scale
docs.text:
Command-line values take precedence over the instrument profile, which takes precedence over the frame header. To solve an image whose header lacks the pointing or the pixel scale, specify them:

fayde solve --image FRAME --ra RA --dec DEC --scale SCALE --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o OUTPUT

Replace the following:

  • RA and DEC: The right ascension and declination of the image center in degrees
  • SCALE: The pixel scale in arcseconds per pixel

When you solve a source list without a frame header, Fayde also needs the image size. Add --width and --height, in pixels, unless the source list has the IMAGEW and IMAGEH keywords.

To decide whether you need these options, check the frame header. Fayde reads keywords such as the following:

Information Header keywords Pointing Image center projected through a supported header WCS, otherwise its reference coordinates (CRVAL1, CRVAL2), RA and DEC, or OBJCTRA and OBJCTDEC Pixel scale XPIXSZ with FOCALLEN, the CD matrix, CDELT1 and CDELT2, PIXSCALE, or SECPIX Observation time JD-OBS, MJD-OBS, or DATE-OBS, with EXPTIME or EXPOSURE Image size NAXIS1 and NAXIS2

If the header has no observation time and you don't set the epoch, Fayde uses the catalog positions at epoch J2000.0 and adds a warning that starts with no observation time to the report. To set the epoch, use --epoch.

Fayde searches within 2° of the pointing. To change the limit, use --radius. To specify the pointing accuracy, use --pointing-sigma with the 1σ error in degrees. When that error is at most a sixth of the limit and the pixel scale is known to within 3%, Fayde first searches within 3σ of the pointing. It widens the search to the limit only when it finds no solution there.

To ignore the pointing and pixel scale from a WCS in the frame header, for example a WCS that another plate solver wrote, add --no-header-wcs. Fayde then reads the header pointing only from RA and DEC, or from OBJCTRA and OBJCTDEC.

To list every option and its default value, run fayde solve --help.

docs.title: Use an instrument profile
docs.text:
An instrument profile is a JSON file with settings that frames from one instrument share: the pixel scale, parity, a rule for deriving the roll from a header keyword, and the pointing accuracy in the frame headers. To use a profile, add --instrument:

fayde solve --image FRAME --instrument PROFILE --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o OUTPUT

Replace PROFILE with the path to the profile file.

All of the following profile fields are optional:

Field Meaning name A name for the profile. The report shows it in priors.instrument. scale_arcsec The pixel scale of an unbinned frame, in arcseconds per pixel scale_sigma_arcsec The 1σ uncertainty of scale_arcsec, in arcseconds per pixel. The default is 0.5% of scale_arcsec. parity negative for an image that shows the sky as seen, with east to the left when north is up, or positive for a mirrored image roll The rule that gives the roll from a header keyword, with these fields: keyword, the header keyword that holds the instrument's roll in degrees; offset_deg and sign, which give the roll as offset_deg + sign × the keyword's value; sigma_deg, the 1σ error of that roll; and max_dev_deg, the hard limit on its deviation. sign is 1 or -1, and the angles are in degrees. binning The header keywords that hold the binning factors, with these fields: x_keyword along x and y_keyword along y. Fayde multiplies the scale and its uncertainty by the square root of the product of the two factors. Without y_keyword, Fayde uses the x factor for both axes. pointing_sigma_deg The 1σ error of the pointing in the frame headers, for each axis, in degrees pointing_radius_deg The search limit around the pointing, in degrees, in place of the default of 2° header_wcs When false, has the same effect as --no-header-wcs on every frame charge_transfer The CCD's charge-transfer smear, which Fayde removes from the positions it detects. For more information, see Correct charge-transfer smear. periodic_pattern Stripes from electronic pickup during readout, which Fayde subtracts before it detects stars. For more information, see Remove a periodic background pattern. source A description of where the values come from. Fayde doesn't read this field.

The roll is the position angle of the image +y axis, measured east of north: atan2(CD1_2, CD2_2). The report's roll_deg field uses the same convention.

The repository contains an example profile, profiles/example.json. A release archive has the same file in the extracted archive's profiles directory. The example's values are illustrative. To create a profile for your instrument, follow these steps:

  1. Copy profiles/example.json.
  2. Edit the copy with your instrument's values. The source field of the example explains the scale and roll values.
  3. If your frame headers lack the keywords that binning names, delete binning from the copy.

Without those keywords, Fayde doesn't use the profile's pixel scale for the frame.

  1. If your frame headers lack the keyword that roll names, delete roll from the copy.

Without that keyword, Fayde doesn't use the profile's roll for the frame.

If you don't know your instrument's values, use Fayde to measure them from its solved frames.

docs.title: Calibrate an instrument profile
docs.text:
You don't need another plate solver to calibrate a profile. For the initial solves, you need the pointing in the frame headers and an approximate pixel scale. To create a profile from these solutions, follow these steps:

  1. In a terminal, solve at least five frames with an approximate pixel scale:
fayde solve --image FRAME --scale SCALE --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o WCS

Replace the following:

  • SCALE: The pixel scale in arcseconds per pixel, correct to within 5%
  • WCS: The path to the WCS file to write, for example frame.wcs. Use a different path for each frame.

For each frame whose report has solved set to true, Fayde writes the solution to WCS. More frames give a better profile.

  1. In a text file, list only the frames whose report has solved set to true, with one frame per line. Each line contains the path to the FITS image, a tab character, and the path to its WCS file, in that order.

  2. In a terminal, create the profile from the list with fayde calibrate:

fayde calibrate --solved LIST --roll-keyword ROLL_KEYWORD --binning XBINNING,YBINNING -o PROFILE

Replace the following:

  • LIST: The path to the text file from the previous step
  • ROLL_KEYWORD: The header keyword that holds the instrument's roll angle in degrees
  • PROFILE: The path to the profile to write, for example camera.json

If the headers have no roll keyword, omit --roll-keyword. If the headers don't record the binning in XBINNING and YBINNING, omit --binning or name the keywords that they use.

Fayde prints the profile and writes it to PROFILE.

A calibrated profile has the following fields:

Field Meaning scale_arcsec, scale_sigma_arcsec The median pixel scale of the solutions and its 1σ uncertainty, in arcseconds per pixel. With --binning, this is the scale of an unbinned frame. parity The parity of the solutions. Fayde omits this field when the solutions disagree. roll With --roll-keyword, the rule that gives the roll from the roll keyword, with its 1σ error and hard limit in degrees binning With --binning, the binning keywords that you named pointing_sigma_deg The 1σ error of the pointing in the headers, in degrees. Fayde omits this field when fewer than five headers have a pointing. charge_transfer With --charge-transfer, the CCD's charge-transfer smear. Fayde omits this field when the frames show no smear. calibration The numbers behind these values: frames used, spreads, and largest deviations

You can add the pointing_radius_deg and header_wcs fields manually. To include header_wcs in the profile during calibration, add --no-header-wcs to the fayde calibrate command.

docs.title: Correct charge-transfer smear
docs.text:
A CCD moves each pixel's charge across the chip to its readout. Traps in the silicon hold back part of the charge and release it later, behind the rest. A star's measured position therefore moves away from the readout edge. The shift is larger for stars farther from that edge, and larger for faint stars than for bright ones. The WCS fit can't absorb a shift that depends on brightness, so it remains in the residuals. Radiation damage adds traps over time, so the smear can grow over the years.

To measure the smear, add --charge-transfer to the fayde calibrate command in Calibrate an instrument profile:

fayde calibrate --solved LIST --charge-transfer --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o PROFILE

Each line of LIST must name the FITS image, not only a header, because Fayde detects the stars again. Fayde matches them to the catalog under each frame's solution, and fits how their residuals depend on brightness and on distance from each edge of the frame. Fayde keeps the result only if the shift is positive and at least five times its uncertainty. If it isn't, Fayde prints a warning and omits the field. Calibration needs at least 200 matched stars.

The charge_transfer field has these fields:

Field Meaning axis y if the charge moves along the columns to a row of the frame, or x if it moves along the rows to a column readout_edge low if the charge moves toward row or column 1, or high if it moves toward the last row or column shift_px The shift in pixels per 1,000 transfers per factor of e (2.718) in flux below flux_ref flux_ref The flux, in image units, at and above which Fayde doesn't move a star per_year, epoch The change of shift_px per year, and the Julian year at which shift_px holds. Fayde fits these when at least five dated frames, each with at least six matched stars, span at least 1 year. Frames without an observation time then don't take part.

For a frame observed in Julian year t, the shift is s = shift_px + per_year × (t − epoch), and never less than 0. Without an observation time, Fayde uses shift_px. A star n rows or columns from the readout edge, with flux F, moves away from that edge by s × (n / 1000) × ln(flux_ref / F). A star with a flux of at least flux_ref doesn't move. With readout_edge set to high, Fayde counts n from the last row or column, and the star moves toward row or column 1. Fayde removes that shift from every star that it detects: with fayde solve, fayde verify, or fayde refit and --image, and with fayde detect --instrument PROFILE. Fayde doesn't change the positions in a source list that you give with --sources, because it calibrates the term against the flux that its own detection measures.

docs.title: Remove a periodic background pattern
docs.text:
Some cameras pick up electronic interference while they read out a frame. The interference adds a wave of fixed frequency to every frame, which appears as fine stripes. Stripes a fraction of the noise high raise the measured noise, so faint stars go undetected. They also line up noise peaks along the stripes, which can make Fayde take a frame of trailed stars for something else.

To find the stripes, add --periodic-pattern to the fayde calibrate command in Calibrate an instrument profile:

fayde calibrate --solved LIST --periodic-pattern -o PROFILE

Each line of LIST must name the FITS image. Fayde averages the power spectra of the frames' backgrounds and keeps up to four peaks that stand far above the rest. If it finds none, it prints a warning and omits the field. Otherwise the profile gets a periodic_pattern field with a frequencies list. Each frequency is a pair of numbers, in cycles per pixel along x and y.

With such a profile, Fayde fits each wave's amplitude and phase in 32 × 32 pixel tiles of every frame, away from the stars, and subtracts the waves before it detects stars. The detection report's periodic_pattern field gives the frequencies, the RMS of what Fayde subtracted (rms), and each wave's mean amplitude (amplitude), in image units. Without such a profile, periodic_pattern is null. If you give --periodic-pattern and --charge-transfer together, Fayde subtracts the pattern before it measures the charge-transfer smear.

A frame that is binned differently can have the stripes at another frequency. At a frequency with no stripes, the fitted amplitude is near zero and the frame barely changes.

docs.title: Solve without a pointing or scale
docs.text:
When you know the pointing and have a precise pixel scale, Fayde needs only the catalog. In that case, omit --index. Fayde searches a pattern index only if it finds no solution around the pointing. This extra search delays the report when a frame has no solution. When the pointing or scale is uncertain or unknown, Fayde also needs a pattern index, which you build once from the catalog. To build the recommended indexes, see Build pattern indexes.

To solve with a pattern index and ignore all priors, use --index and --no-priors:

fayde solve --image FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --index INDEX --no-priors -o OUTPUT

Replace INDEX with the path to a pattern index, for example allsky-1.0.fidx. To use several indexes, add --index once for each file.

docs.title: Limit the search time
docs.text:
Search time increases with the area within the pointing radius. The following measurements show exhausted searches of real frames on a 32-core x86_64 Linux computer, with the pixel scale known to 0.1% and the roll unconstrained:

Pointing radius Hypotheses until exhausted Time 0.5° 250–760 0.01–0.02 s 1° 830–2,500 0.02–0.05 s 2° 2,900–10,500 0.07–0.16 s 4° 11,000–40,000 0.24–0.62 s 8° 47,000–157,000 0.9–2.3 s

A search with a 1° radius takes about 50 times less work than one with an 8° radius. Frames with hundreds of sources took more than 18 s at an 8° radius. To limit a search, use these options:

  • Use --max-hypotheses to limit the work independently of the computer's speed.
  • Use --deadline to limit elapsed search time. For image input the clock starts after the initial source detection. A retry with point detections shares the remaining time and hypothesis budget. Fayde checks the deadline again after measuring the points.

Each search stage in the report ends with an outcome: solved, exhausted, deadline, or hypothesis limit. When Fayde finds no solution, the report names the stage that a limit stopped.

docs.title: Read the report
docs.text:
The fayde solve and fayde refit commands use the same report fields. The fields present depend on the outcome:

  • With a solution, the report has solved set to true and the fields in the following table, except reason, error, best_log_odds, warnings, and detection.
  • When a search finishes without a solution, the report has solved set to false, reason, best_log_odds, hypotheses_tested, search, priors, and identity.
  • After a solver error, the report has solved set to false, error set to true, reason, priors, and identity.

Each report also has warnings when there are warnings, and detection when you give an image with --image. Pixel positions in the report are 1-based, as in FITS.

To state the uncertainty of a solution, quote worst_sigma_arcsec. It's the largest predicted position error at the sampled positions across the frame.

Field Meaning solved true when Fayde found a solution that passed verification reason Why Fayde found no solution, or the error error true when the solver failed crval_deg The right ascension and declination of the image center, in degrees. The WCS has its reference pixel at the image center. pixel_scale_arcsec The pixel scale at the image center, in arcseconds per pixel roll_deg The position angle of the image +y axis, measured east of north, in degrees from −180° to 180°: atan2(CD1_2, CD2_2) parity Negative for an image that shows the sky as seen, with east to the left when north is up, or Positive for a mirrored image centre_sigma_arcsec The predicted radial 1σ position error at the image center, in arcseconds worst_sigma_arcsec The largest predicted radial 1σ position error on a 5 × 5 grid that covers the frame, corners included, in arcseconds rms_px The root mean square (RMS) residual of the matched sources, weighted by their inlier probability, in pixels loo_rms_px The leave-one-out RMS residual of the confident matches, in pixels: each match's residual from a fit without it. The value is null when there are too few matches. error_scale The factor that the fit applies to the source position errors. A value greater than 1 means that the errors were too small. matches The number of matched sources log_odds The natural logarithm of the odds of the solution against sources at random positions best_log_odds Without a solution, the highest log_odds that a hypothesis reached, or null nfa Model-based false-alarm score, hypotheses_tested × exp(−log_odds). Calibration of the adaptive search requires null trials. method How Fayde found the solution: PairSeeds from star pairs around the pointing, PatternHash from a pattern index, or Refit from the WCS that you gave index_hash The content hash of the pattern index that found the solution, or null solved_by_stage The name of the search stage that found the solution sip_order The order of the SIP distortion polynomial, or 1 when the solution has no distortion terms priors The priors that Fayde used, and in each prior's origin field, where the prior came from: the command line, the instrument profile, or a header keyword. It also gives the instrument profile's name, the trail, the number of truncated sources, and the default position error. warnings Header values that Fayde didn't use, and options that --no-priors or --no-pointing dropped. When the header has no observation time and you don't set the epoch, a warning starts with no observation time, and Fayde uses the catalog positions at epoch J2000.0. prior_violated, violated_priors Whether the solution breaks a hard limit of the priors, and which: pointing, scale, roll, or parity. This can happen only with --search-outside-pointing or --relax-priors-on-failure. relaxed_priors true when the solution comes from the retry with wider limits that --relax-priors-on-failure allows hypotheses_tested The number of hypotheses tested search The search stages in order. Each stage has stage, hypotheses, seconds, and outcome. seconds The wall-clock time of the solve, in seconds wcs_cards The solution as 80-character FITS header cards, including IMAGEW and IMAGEH pairs The matched sources. Each pair has the source's index in the source list (source) and position (x, y), the catalog star's UCAC4 running number (star_id), position at the solve epoch (ra_deg, dec_deg), and magnitude (mag), the star's predicted position (predicted_x, predicted_y), the source position minus the predicted position in pixels (residual_px), and the probability that the match is real (inlier_prob). covariance The covariance of the fitted coefficients, the same for each tangent-plane axis. matrix_rad2 is the matrix row by row, in square radians. terms gives the powers of the pixel offsets from crpix_fits, divided by norm_px, that the coefficients multiply. detection The detection report without its source lists or its separate identity field. For more information about its fields, see Read the detection report. identity The Fayde version and commit, the catalog and the solve epoch, and the pattern indexes with their content hashes

In a fayde verify report, accepted is true when log_odds reaches threshold. The report also has matches, confident_matches, rms_px, references, sources, pairs, priors, and identity.

docs.title: Read the detection report
docs.text:
The fayde detect command prints a detection report. The detection field in a fayde solve --image report omits the sources and rejected lists and the detection report's separate identity field.

The mode field is points, trails, kernel, or refused. For more information about these values, see Detect stars without solving. The census field holds the evidence for the decision. Its reason field has one of the following values:

reason mode Meaning no elongated sources points No bright source is elongated. no common trail direction points Too few elongated sources share one direction. trails shorter than 7 FWHM points The trails are shorter than seven times the stars' full width at half maximum (FWHM) across the trail. one straight trail trails Every star is a straight trail of one length and direction. shared curved star path kernel The template learned from the stars has a measurable bend. star paths vary with field rotation kernel The star trails are tangential to a common center and grow longer with distance from it. point stars as well as trails (...) refused The image has round stars as well as trails. The reason gives the number of each. two trail populations refused The trails have two directions. To choose one, use --trail-angle. trails longer than the frame refused Most trails touch the frame edge, so Fayde can't measure their length. too little light for the second estimate refused The image has too little light for a second, independent estimate of the trail. the two estimates disagree refused Two independent estimates of the trail disagree. the trails change across the frame refused The trail direction or length differs between regions of the frame. too few trails to check that they are straight refused Fayde fitted too few trails to check that they're straight.

The trail field is null except in trails mode, when it contains the following fields:

Field Meaning length_px The full length of the trail, in pixels angle_deg The direction of the trail, in degrees from +x toward +y, from −90° to 90° width_sigma_px The Gaussian σ of the stars across the trail, in pixels sigma_length_px The 1σ error of length_px, in pixels sigma_angle_deg The 1σ error of angle_deg, in degrees fitted The number of trails that Fayde fitted to measure the trail. When the value is 0, Fayde uses the census values.

The kernel field contains the following measurements in kernel mode. Its value is null in the other modes.

Field Meaning width_px, height_px Bounding dimensions of the correlation taps. For field rotation, these are the maximum dimensions over the regions. stacked Number of stars that contributed to the template or common transverse profile. path_length_px Estimated path length. For field rotation, this is the median over the regions. bend_px RMS deviation of the path from its best straight line. For field rotation, this is the median over the regions. regions Number of regions with distinct templates.

The sources field lists the stars that Fayde passes to the solver, and the rejected field lists the detections that it set aside. Each detection has a 1-based position (x, y), a 1σ position error (sigma_px), and 1σ errors along the trail (sigma_along_px) and across it (sigma_across_px). In trails mode, a star's sigma_px is the larger of sigma_along_px and sigma_across_px. In kernel mode, the errors are along and across the template's major axis, and sigma_px is the largest 1σ error over all directions. When the stars are points, the three errors are equal. The class field describes each detection.

  • In sources: star, saturated for a star with saturated pixels, or extended for a source that is wider than the stars
  • In rejected: sharp for a hot pixel or cosmic-ray hit, streak for a detection on a traced streak, or point for a point-like source in an image whose stars are trails, such as the tracked object

With a profile that has a charge_transfer field, the positions in sources are corrected. Each star's charge_transfer_px field holds the shift that Fayde removed, in pixels. The report's charge_transfer field holds the term that Fayde used, the shift at the frame's epoch, the number of stars moved (moved), and the largest shift (max_px). Without such a profile, charge_transfer is null.

docs.title: Check or refit an existing WCS
docs.text:
To check a WCS from any solver against the catalog, use fayde verify:

fayde verify --image FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --wcs WCS

To fit the WCS again from the matched stars and write the result, use fayde refit:

fayde refit --image FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --wcs WCS -o OUTPUT

Replace the following:

  • WCS: The path to the WCS file to check, for example frame.wcs
  • OUTPUT: The path to the WCS file to write, which must differ from WCS

Both commands also accept a source list: use --sources SOURCES --header FRAME in place of --image FRAME.

docs.title: Find catalog stars at a position
docs.text:
To find catalog stars at positions under a given WCS, use fayde verify. Specify pixel positions with --at, sky positions with --at-sky, or a source list with --at-sources.

To check positions from a source list, use --at-sources:

fayde verify --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --wcs WCS --header FRAME --at-sources SOURCES

To check a pixel position and a sky position at a specified epoch, use --at and --at-sky:

fayde verify --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --wcs WCS --epoch 2020.89 --at 412.3,88.1 --at-sky 172.5,1.6

Pixel positions are 1-based, as in FITS: the center of the first pixel is at (1, 1). Sky positions are the right ascension and declination in degrees.

For each position, the report lists the following:

  • The nearest stars at the observation epoch and their separations
  • The combined 1σ uncertainty of the position, catalog, and WCS (--wcs-sigma)
  • The probability of an offset this large or larger if the position is the star (p_consistent)
  • The probability that some star lies this close to an arbitrary position (p_chance)

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: Fayde follows semantic versioning. While the version is 0.x, a breaking change increases the minor number, and anything else increases the patch number.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
The following changes are breaking:

  • Removing a command-line or Python option, or changing its meaning
  • Removing or renaming a JSON report field
  • Changing the index file format or the bytes of an index, including its content_hash
  • Changing a published crate's public Rust API so that existing code no longer compiles (for example, adding a field to a public struct without #[non_exhaustive])

Adding a report field isn't a breaking change. If a release changes indexes, you must rebuild your indexes as directed in the release notes.

A fix that leaves reports and indexes unchanged is a patch release. So is a new command, option, or report field that changes nothing that already exists.

docs.title: Deprecations
docs.text:
Before Fayde removes or renames a command-line option, a Python argument, or a report field, one release deprecates it:

  1. The release that deprecates it still accepts the old name and behaves as before. Fayde prints a warning that names the replacement, and the release notes list the deprecation.
  2. A later breaking release removes it, no earlier than the next minor version.

A change that can't keep the old behavior, such as a new index format, can't be deprecated first. Its release notes say what to do, for example to rebuild your indexes.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text: Each release has a section in the changelog that lists its changes and marks the breaking ones. The same version is published on GitHub, PyPI, and crates.io.

docs.title: Star and streak detection — design
docs.text: Crate fayde-detect. Survey of existing methods: docs/research/literature-review.md §7. Sources of every algorithm: docs/references.md.

docs.title: 1. Scope
docs.text:
Input: one image whose stars are points (a frame tracked at the sidereal rate, or a spacecraft holding its attitude), with possibly a satellite streak or two, hot pixels, cosmic-ray hits, saturated stars, stray light. Output: what the solver's input contract asks of a source list (plate-solver.md §6.3), filled honestly:

Per source How it is obtained x, y Closed-form fit to the peak of the matched-filtered image (§3.4) sigma_px Noise theory of that estimator, per source (§4) flux Integral of the fitted Gaussian p_star Local false discovery rate × shape class (§3.8) truncated The fit window reaches the frame edge

Streaks are traced and reported (ends, angle, width, flux), and every detection on one is kept out of the star list. Frames whose stars are trailed (tracking a satellite) are handled by a second pass, designed in streak-detection.md.

Design targets, in order: no parameter the user must know (star width, noise and threshold are measured or derived; gain is read from the header when it is there); robust to cosmic rays by the hundred and to stray light; position errors that the solver's verification and fit can trust; speed; and the same bits on every machine (fayde_core::Portable, no platform math).

docs.title: 2. Why not an existing detector
docs.text:
From the survey (literature review §7) of the detectors in use:

  • None measures the star width and adapts its filter. astrometry.net's simplexy smooths with a fixed σ = 1 px; DAOFIND and photutils need the FWHM from the user; SExtractor a fixed 3 × 3 kernel; cedar-detect a fixed 7-pixel gate with manual binning.
  • None reports a per-star position error to the matcher.
  • None runs a streak detector before solving. Streak fragments are rejected only as a side effect of size or shape gates, and astrometry.net removes only horizontal and vertical lines.
  • Hot pixels and cosmic rays are handled by minimum-area or sharpness heuristics that conflict with undersampled stars.
  • Licenses: SExtractor GPL, SEP LGPL, astrometry.net GPL as distributed, cedar-detect source-available but not open source. Everything here is written from the papers, so no other project's code, and none of its license terms, enters Fayde.

docs.title: 3. Method
docs.text:
image
  │ 1. matched filter (Gaussian; width measured, image binned if stars are wide)
  │ 2. background and noise mesh of the filtered image
  │ 3. peaks: local maxima above the false-alarm threshold
  │ 4. one closed-form fit per peak → position, size, shape, amplitude
  │ 5. local test: each peak against the ring around it
  │ 6. classes: star, saturated, extended, sharp
  │ 7. streaks: traced from ridge-like peaks
  │ 8. probabilities and errors
  ▼
stars (x, y, σ, flux, p_star) + streaks

docs.title: 3.1 Matched filter and scale
docs.text: The image is convolved with a Gaussian of the stars' width, the filter of highest signal-to-noise ratio for a point source in white noise. The width is not asked for. A first pass at σk = 1.2 px (within 7% of the best ratio for stars of FWHM 1.9 to 4.1 px) measures it (§3.3); a second pass is run only when the ratio 2·σk·σp / (σk² + σp²) falls below 0.93. Stars wider than σ = 2 px are binned first (block means), so wide-star frames cost less than narrow-star ones. At most three passes.

docs.title: 3.2 Background and noise
docs.text:
Tiles of 64 px (the same sky area on a binned image, down to 24 binned px), measured on the filtered image so that the noise is that of the thresholded quantity whatever the input's noise correlation.

  • Background: median of a sample of the tile, clipped once at median + 3σ.
  • Noise: 1.4826 × MAD / √2 of the differences of pixel pairs separated by more than the kernel's reach, clipped up to three times. A difference cancels the background and its gradient, which a spread of values would count as noise.
  • A tile standing above what its neighbors predict (a bright star, a galaxy) is replaced by the prediction: the largest, over the four lines through the tile, of the mean of its two neighbors on that line. SExtractor's 3 × 3 median flattens the corner of a frame lit from outside; this filter does not (the glow of stray light curves up along the direction to its source and down across it, and the line nearest that direction predicts at least the tile).
  • Between tile centers the values are bilinear; beyond the outermost centers the background is extrapolated in a straight line, so a gradient running off the frame is followed to the edge.

If at least a quarter of the valid raw pixels equal the frame minimum, Fayde checks the distribution of those pixels in each tile. A tile is padding if at least 99% of its valid pixels equal the floor, or if transitions between floor and above-floor pixels occur at most a quarter as often as in a random mix. The detector checks the transition rate in tiles with at least eight floor pixels.

Fayde uses the clipped-sky model when more than half of the sky tiles with at least 24 valid pixels yield a fit. To fit a tile, at least a quarter of its valid pixels must be at the floor and at least 16 must be above it. The singly left-censored normal fit uses the floor fraction and an empirical quantile near the middle of the surviving values. Tiles without a fit use the frame's typical fit. When the model applies, floor pixels in padding tiles are undefined for detection. Otherwise, Fayde uses the standard filtered mesh.

The fit estimates the sky before clipping. Its clipped moments give the background and noise of the recorded pixels. Fayde propagates these through the point filter and accounts for the skew of the filtered noise when setting peak and census thresholds. The trail pass uses the same sky model for raw-pixel fits and to set a minimum noise scale for the aimed filter. On a clipped frame, the automatic trail threshold is at least 5σ, and a trail center must be on the frame and have an along-trail uncertainty within one FWHM across the trail.

docs.title: 3.3 Star width
docs.text:
For a peak of the filtered image, the variance of the star's profile is the fitted variance (§3.4) less the kernel's. The frame's star width is taken from bright, round peaks, but they are not all stars: on a warm or irradiated detector hot pixels and cosmic-ray hits outnumber stars ten to one or more. Nothing that came through the optics is sharper than the optics allow, and stars share one width where artifacts have many. So the stars are the widest distinct mode of the size distribution: in a histogram of ln(size), the widest local maximum holding at least 5% of the tallest one's count and separated from narrower sizes by a dip to half its height. Blends and galaxies form a tail, not a mode.

The stars' shape is measured with their width: the median narrow-axis variance and the median axis ratio of the peaks in that mode. A drift during the exposure smears every star alike. Each source's narrow axis is then well under the stars' mean width, so narrowness (§3.6) and elongation (§3.6, §3.7) are judged against what the frame's stars show, not against a round star of the mean width.

docs.title: 3.4 One fit per peak
docs.text:
A quadratic surface is fitted by least squares to the logarithm of the 3 × 3 filtered pixels around the maximum. For an elliptical Gaussian this is exact, and it gives at once:

  • the position (no pixel-phase bias, unlike a quadratic fitted to the values themselves, whose bias reaches 0.03 px for these widths);
  • the variances along both axes and the orientation (eigen-decomposition of the fitted Hessian H: variance along an axis = −1/eigenvalue);
  • the amplitude, and so the flux 2π·A·σmajor·σminor.

Cost: nine logarithms and about 40 multiplications per peak.

docs.title: 3.5 Local test
docs.text: The mesh follows the frame on the scale of its tiles. Stray light and halos change faster, and what the mesh misses is left as broad bumps. A star is narrow: three widths from its center nothing of it is left, so its height above the median of a ring of that radius (eight samples, robust to a neighbor or a streak crossing the ring) is its height; a bump two or more star-widths across falls short. Where the ring agrees with the mesh, the mesh (less noisy) stands; elsewhere the ring is the background and the peak must exceed it by the threshold less one σ. Saturated stars are exempt.

docs.title: 3.6 Classes
docs.text:
Class Test Goes to the solver sharp Narrowest axis under 0.4 of the stars' narrow-axis variance, beyond the fit's noise; or, in the unfiltered pixels, the second faintest of the four neighbors of the brightest pixel under half of exp(−1/σ²) of it (light through the optics reaches all four; charge deposited in the detector does not) no saturated Top at the saturation level (given, from the header, or the level of flat tops at the frame's brightest) yes, p × 0.9 extended Elongated over 1.5 times the stars' own axis ratio, or over twice the stars' variance, beyond the fit's noise yes, p × 0.5 streak On a traced streak no point Point-like in a frame whose stars are trails (the tracked object): streak-detection.md no star The rest yes

A saturated star's center is the mean position of the core of its saturated region: the pixels whose runs of saturated pixels along the row and along the column are each at least half the longest. A bleed trail, a few pixels wide, has short runs across it and does not move the center. A saturated region that is a line of even width is a streak, not a star.

The work is bounded whatever the frame and the settings: each saturated pixel is flooded once per frame, a region is followed for at most 200,000 pixels, a saturation level within 20σ of the background is ignored, at most 200,000 peaks are measured and 1,000 streaks traced, and binning never leaves an image under 16 pixels on a side.

docs.title: 3.7 Streaks
docs.text:
A peak on a streak is a ridge: the fitted surface curves down across the streak and hardly at all along it. Each ridge-like peak (axis ratio at least twice the stars') seeds a trace: the ridge is followed one pixel at a time in both directions along a straight line refitted by least squares as points are added, re-centring on the brightest of five samples across the track, bridging gaps in proportion to the length traced. Holding the trace to a line keeps it on course past a bright star beside the streak or another streak crossing it. Then:

  • isolated points at the ends, short groups beyond a gap, and a bright star touching an end are removed;
  • the line is a total-least-squares fit; each end is put where the ridge falls to half its level (the true end of a uniform streak blurred by the PSF);
  • the streak is traced once more from the middle of the fitted line, whose direction is better than the seed's;
  • it is kept if it is at least 10 px and 8 cross-section σ long, half covered, with a total signal-to-noise ratio of 10, and if at least half of the bright peaks on it are ridges (a row of stars is not a streak);
  • a streak narrower than the stars is flagged cosmic_ray.

Only streaks bright enough to raise a peak above the detection threshold are found (about 5σ per PSF area). Fainter ones do not disturb the star list. Fayde does not search for them: an integration along the line (Radon transform; Nir, Zackay & Ofek 2018) costs 10 to 100 times everything here.

docs.title: 3.8 Threshold and probabilities
docs.text:
The threshold is set from the number of noise peaks the caller accepts per frame (default 1): the expected number of local maxima of filtered noise above u per pixel is bounded by min(P(Z > u), u·φ(u) / (4π·σk²)), the pixel count and the peak density of a continuous Gaussian field. On empty synthetic frames the bound is within 45% of the count for σk from 0.7 to 2 px. For a 4-megapixel frame the threshold is 5.0σ.

p_star = (1 − local false discovery rate) × class factor. The local rate is the expected number of noise peaks within a quarter σ of a source's height over the number of sources seen there. A source at the threshold in an empty region of height gets a low probability; the same height among many real faint stars gets a high one.

docs.title: 4. Position error
docs.text:
The position is the maximum of the filtered image. Noise moves a maximum by (noise gradient) / (signal curvature). For white noise σn filtered by a Gaussian of σk, and a Gaussian star whose filtered profile has variance σt² = σp² + σk² and peak A:

Var(∂n/∂x) = N² / (2σk²),  N = filtered noise;   curvature = A / σt²
σx = σt² / (√2 · σk · SNR),  SNR = A / N

For a matched kernel (σk = σp) this is √2·σp / SNR, the Cramér–Rao bound for a Gaussian star in background noise (0.60 FWHM / SNR). Everything in it is measured per source.

The star's own photon noise, with gain g given (N electrons): the same calculation with noise variance proportional to the star's profile gives

Var = σp² · σt⁸ / (N · σk⁴ · (σk² + 2σp²)²)     = (16/9) · σp² / N  for a matched kernel

the known result for a Gaussian-weighted centroid (Mortensen et al. 2010, eq. 6). Without a gain it is not modeled, and a floor of 0.05 px stands in. Saturated stars: 0.1 px + 3% of the radius of the saturated core (measured on synthetic frames).

docs.title: 5. Measured
docs.text:
Synthetic frames (fayde_detect::synth: pixel-integrated Gaussian or Moffat stars, sky and read noise, photon noise, streaks, hot pixels, cosmic rays, stray light, saturation). One laptop core.

Quantity Result Speed, 4 Mpx frame, stars of σ 1.5 px 10 ms (2.4 ms/Mpx), one pass Speed, stars of σ 0.6 / 2.5 / 4 / 8 px 4 to 7 ms/Mpx (two or three passes; binned from σ 2.5 px up) Star width within 1% of the truth, σ 0.6 to 8 px Noise within 1% on sparse frames; reads up to 12% high when stars cover much of the frame Completeness every star above SNR 8; 21 of 28 between SNR 5 and 8 Error / claimed error (robust spread; gain given) 0.8 to 1.25 for σ 0.9, 1.5, 2.6 px Error / Cramér–Rao bound, faint stars 0.8 to 1.3 False stars on empty frames 3 in six 4 Mpx frames at the default (1 per frame asked) Hot pixels (60 per frame) flagged 60 of 60 at σ 0.7 and 1.5 px; 55 of 60 at σ 3 px (binned) Cosmic rays, 15 to 30 hits per star 0.3 to 0.6% of hits pass as faint stars at σ 1.5 px, 0.8% at σ 1.0 px; star width unaffected Stray light, 20 × sky from a corner 1 false star; without the local test, 33 Streak ends within 2 px (0.2 px typical); faint streaks (5σ ridge) within 10 px Saturated stars, 3 to 300 × saturation, with bleed trails center within 0.6 px; one detection each

End to end (crates/fayde-api/tests/image_solve.rs, a synthetic sky through a known WCS, two streaks, hot pixels, saturated stars): worst sky error over the frame 0.11″ at 3″/px for well-sampled stars (0.035 px), 0.08″ undersampled, 0.49″ for seeing-limited stars 7 px wide. The solver's fitted error scale is 1.01 on the well-sampled frame: the claimed errors are the real ones.

Real frames: 109 frames whose stars are points (two pixel scales; 3 to 10 s exposures, stars of FWHM 2.2 to 3.3 px, 4 to 540 hot pixels and radiation hits per frame, up to 4 streaks or cosmic-ray tracks in most frames), solved from the image file alone against UCAC4 with the header pointing (2° radius) and a scale prior:

Solved 109 of 109 Detection time 2.0 ms per frame (median). A later run measured 2.2 ms, and 3.0 ms with the trail census (streak-detection.md §7) Matched stars 181 (median) Residual 0.40 px RMS (median) Error scale fitted by the solver 1.58 (median): on these frames the claimed errors are too small by that factor, with or without the gain

Two of those frames shaped the method:

  • One, taken with a warm detector, has 300 radiation hits to 36 stars among its bright compact sources. It is what the widest-mode rule (§3.3) was made for.
  • One is a crowded field whose stars are smeared two to one by a drift. With narrowness judged against the stars' mean width, its 36 brightest stars were classed as cosmic rays (117 "sharp" sources; 7 once judged against the stars' narrow axis), and with the brightest stars missing the solver's search, which starts from them, found nothing although 417 of the remaining sources matched the catalog. It now solves with 451 matched stars.

The detector this one replaced (after SExtractor: clipped-mode mesh, pixel cleaning, matched filter, connected pixels, windowed centroids) was run on the same 109 frames with the same solver and priors: 105 solved, median residual 0.79 px, error scale 2.65, about 20 ms per frame. On the 105 frames both solve, the field centers agree to 0.19″ (median); on the one where they differ by 10″, this detector's solution has a residual of 1.5 px and the other's 5 px.

docs.title: 6. Limits
docs.text:
1. Faint streaks (under about 5σ per PSF area) are not found (§3.7).
  2. With stars of FWHM under about 2.5 px, multi-pixel cosmic-ray clumps of signal-to-noise ratio under about 30 cannot be told from faint stars by a 3 × 3 shape: in the worst synthetic case (3000 hits, 200 stars of FWHM 2.4 px, stray light and streaks together) 8% of the hits pass as faint stars. They are distractors the solver is built for.
  3. The claimed position errors assume a Gaussian core and white noise. On real frames the solver's error scale shows them 1.5 times too small; the cause (pixel response, PSF shape, pointing jitter) has not been separated.
  4. Undersampled stars (σ under 0.7 px): errors about 1.3 times the claim.
  5. One thread. The filter and the scan split into strips without changing the result.
  6. FITS images only (8 to 64-bit integers and floats); tile-compressed images are not read.
  7. Trailed stars (from a telescope tracking a satellite) are handled by a second pass: streak-detection.md §7.

docs.title: Fayde plate solver — design
docs.text: For the crate layout and integration contract, see §4 and §6. For commands and report fields, see the CLI guide and Python guide. Source references in the prior-art survey (§3) point to the upstream repositories.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Fayde is a public, open-source astrometry tool written in Rust. It goes from a source list to a verified WCS with measured accuracy. It must fully meet the needs of a host pipeline, so that the pipeline can retire solve-field and the solving-related code around it.

The input is an xylist, as with solve-field, or an image. The user can run whatever source detector suits their sensor and give Fayde the resulting list of sources (§6) along with any header or metadata they have. Fayde also takes the image itself when its stars are points (a frame tracked at the sidereal rate, a spacecraft holding its attitude), detects the stars, keeps streaks and artifacts out of the list, and fills the same contract: detection.md. It does the same when every star is a trail of one length and direction (a telescope tracking a satellite): streak-detection.md.

It is not a wrapper. It ports the strongest algorithms from three solvers, and it takes over capabilities that pipelines otherwise build around a solver, generalized for public use:

Concern Taken from Reason Fast hinted match tetra3 / cedar-solve; Mortari's pair lists Pair seeds when the scale is tight, otherwise a 4-star edge-ratio pattern hash; millisecond solves Blind / wide fallback astrometry.net, adapted Its series of indexes for different field widths, searched with Fayde's 5-ratio pattern hash (quad codes considered, not adopted) Match acceptance astrometry.net Bayesian log-odds verification against the catalog Final fit astrometry.net, extended TAN + SIP fit, upgraded to weighted iterative refit with outlier rejection Source detection Fayde's own, for point-like and trailed stars; otherwise the user supplies the xylist One fixed extractor cannot fit every sensor; astrometry.net's built-in simplexy solved about 12% of one host pipeline's frames. Fayde defines a rich xylist contract (§6) that any detector can fill, and fills it itself from an image of point-like stars with a detector that measures the star width, noise and position errors instead of asking for them (detection.md). Catalog Fayde's own UCAC4 and Tycho-2 read natively behind a catalog trait Header priors, neighbor hints Fayde's own Scale and pointing resolution and a prediction from a solved neighbor, which a pipeline otherwise builds around the solver

docs.title: Standalone first, host pipelines first-class
docs.text:
Fayde is a general-purpose public tool. A host pipeline is a user, not a dependency. Fayde takes on capabilities that pipelines otherwise build around a solver when they belong in a public astrometry tool.

Detection of point-like and trailed stars is one of them. A host may still prefer its own detector and give the xylist.

In Fayde (so that a host pipeline need not build them):

Capability Fayde home Star and streak detection from the image, points or trails fayde-detect Source ranking and demotion of near-duplicate centroids fayde-solve (§5.0) Scale prior from focal length and pixel size, or from CD or PC+CDELT with unit checks; rejection of mixed or invalid WCS fayde-fits Pointing prior from the header, never treating a commanded WCS as solved fayde-fits Exposure time resolution (DATE-OBS, JD-OBS, TIME-OBS, EXPTIME and variants) fayde-fits UCAC4 cone search; "is there a catalog star here?" check fayde-catalog (cone search) + fayde verify --at Verifying or repairing existing WCS headers fayde verify, fayde refit Writing the solution atomically as a separate FITS WCS file, leaving the image untouched fayde-fits (WCS file), fayde-cli (provenance cards)

These stay in the host pipeline, as pipeline policy rather than astrometry:

  • WCS cache reuse policy, versioned header cards and policy fingerprints.
  • Run-summary and evidence schemas.
  • Satellite identification, correlation, stacking, and drift.
  • A detector of the host's own, where it prefers one to Fayde's.

A host's solving path is then: its detector → xylist → Fayde → adapter → its own cache and records.

General rules:

  • Core crates know nothing about any host pipeline: no host field names, config keys, cache records or FITS history cards.
  • Fayde's own inputs and outputs are general: a source list, hints, and a solution with full evidence. They are designed so that everything a host pipeline needs maps onto them with no loss (§6).
  • A host adapter is thin and lives at the edge: fayde-py plus a backend in the host's own repository. Host-specific provenance (cache records, run summaries) is built there from Fayde's generic provenance.
  • Other users get the same features through the CLI and the Rust API. These include ground telescopes, star trackers, and any solve-field user who is willing to switch.

docs.title: Why not keep astrometry.net
docs.text:
• Maintenance is sporadic; build and packaging are C/Python/SWIG and hard to vendor.
  • Every solve is a subprocess with scratch files, a 180 s budget and text-file I/O.
  • It does not expose solution covariance, so the accuracy of an accepted solution is not quantified.
  • Index files are fixed 2MASS/Tycho-2/Gaia-DR2 builds (series 4200/5200); epoch handling is not declared, and we cannot build from UCAC4 with our own epoch and density policy.
  • No native notion of an image sequence; a pipeline has to implement neighbor hints and borrowing around it.

docs.title: Must
docs.text:
1. Define an input contract optimized for solution quality (§6). Only the sources and image size are required. Every other field (uncertainties, flux, p_star, exposure time, priors with σ) improves the result when present. Internally, (x, y) = (column, row), with the center of the first pixel at (0, 0) (NumPy/Astropy). Conversions happen only at the edges: +1 for FITS/astrometry.net xylists, +0.5 and an (x, y)→(y, x) swap for tetra3/cedar.
  2. Use priors when present: pointing, roll, scale and parity, each given as a σ plus a hard limit. The limit bounds the search; the σ ranks hypotheses (§6.4).
  3. Solve blind (no position hint) within a bounded time when the hint is missing or wrong.
  4. Build indexes from UCAC4 zone files (z001–z900, 78-byte records), with proper motion propagated to a chosen epoch and per-cell density limiting. Catalog access goes through a trait so Tycho-2, Gaia DR3 and others can be added.
  5. Output a FITS-compatible TAN or TAN-SIP WCS, plus: matched pairs, per-star residuals, RMS, parameter covariance, the log-odds score, index/catalog identity and epoch.
  6. Deterministic: same input, same index → bit-identical output. Required by a host pipeline's WCS cache fingerprints.
  7. Library first (no subprocess), with a CLI and Python bindings for host pipelines.
  8. Read xylists in Fayde's native format (§6.8) and in astrometry.net's FITS xylist format. A solve-field user should be able to point Fayde at their existing .xyls files and get a solution with no other changes.
  9. Build priors (scale, pointing, exposure time) from standard FITS headers with strict validation.
  10. Public tool hygiene: an open source license, documented CLI, published crates and wheels, and reproducible index builds anyone can run from public catalogs.

docs.title: Should
docs.text:
1. Sequence mode: when the search finds no solution, verify a WCS predicted from a solved frame of the same pass.
  2. Per-source centroid uncertainty: each source may carry a position error that the verifier and fitter use (§6.3). Sources are treated as point centroids; producers with streaked stars supply the streak centroid.
  3. Solve the target case (sub-degree FOV, ~3″/px, 30–60 sources) in < 100 ms hinted and < 5 s blind on a single core.

docs.title: Won't
docs.text: • Lens-distortion models beyond SIP (TPV, lookup tables).

docs.title: 3.1 astrometry.net (dstndstn/astrometry.net)
docs.text:
astrometry.net reads an image or a FITS xylist (X, Y, optional FLUX/BACKGROUND). Coordinates are 1-based, so the center of the first pixel is (1, 1) (util/image2xy.c:102-105). The list is sorted brightest first, and --depth limits how many objects are tried. The built-in extractor (simplexy) does median background subtraction, 8σ peaks and a 3×3 centroid (include/astrometry/simplexy.h:10-20).

The hints are the scale in degwidth, arcminwidth, arcsec/px or focal length (solver/augment-xylist.c:83-89), an RA/Dec center with a radius (solver/engine.c:496-576), parity, and a CPU limit.

The pattern is a quad of 4 stars. A and B are the widest pair. C and D are expressed in the frame where A=(0,0) and B=(1,1), giving a 4-D code that does not change under rotation, scaling or translation (solver/quad-utils.c:15-55). Requiring cx ≤ dx and flipping for parity removes duplicate orderings (quad-utils.c:102-150). Code tolerance is 0.01 (solver.h:30). Field stars are added one at a time and every quad containing the new star is tried (solver/solver.c:898-990), using a kd-tree range search in code space.

The index is a set of FITS files, each holding a star kd-tree (unit xyz vectors), a quad table and a code kd-tree. One file covers one band of quad sizes, in steps of √2. The 4100 series (Tycho-2) covers 22′–2000′. The 5200 series covers 2′–22′ and is split into 12 or 48 HEALPix tiles. Small scales need tens of GB. Star density is evened out by uniformize-catalog (N brightest per HEALPix cell, in sweeps) and hpquads.

Verification uses Bayesian log-odds (solver/verify.c:448-620). Each test star is scored either as a true match (a Gaussian) or as a spurious "distractor" star (uniform over the field), with conflicts resolved. Defaults: distractor ratio 0.25, verify_pix 1 px, accept at odds 1e9 (engine.c:672-673).

The output is a full TAN + SIP WCS from tweak2 (solver.c:126-220), plus .corr, .match and .rdls files.

It is the most robust of the three and needs no FOV. It is slow to start (seconds), its indexes are large, and the C/FITS stack is heavy.

Its catalogs are Tycho-2, 2MASS, USNO-B, NOMAD and UCAC3/4/5 (catalogs/). UCAC4 is supported (catalogs/ucac4.c:51-125) through ucac4tofits → hpsplit → build-astrometry-index. It does not propagate proper motion; positions stay at J2000.

docs.title: 3.2 tetra3 (esa/tetra3)
docs.text:
solve_from_image uses its own blob extractor (tetra3.py:1796). solve_from_centroids takes (y, x), with the origin at the top-left pixel edge (so the first pixel center is 0.5), sorted brightest first, plus (height, width).

A pattern of 4 stars gives 6 edges. They are sorted and divided by the longest edge to give 5 ratios, binned at 1/(4·max_err) (tetra3.py:1060-1071). The key is a polynomial over the bins, multiplied by 2654435761, in an open-addressed table with quadratic probing (tetra3.py:110-153). It tries every 4-combination of the brightest 8 centroids (tetra3.py:1381).

The database is an .npz with a star table (float32) and a pattern table of star indices (2× table oversize), about 99 MB. It is built per FOV scale (step 1.5×) with a minimum star separation of 0.6·fov/√stars_per_fov (tetra3.py:925-1013).

Verification finds the rotation by SVD (Kabsch) with no determinant check, so it can accept a mirror-image (wrong parity) solution (tetra3.py:236-244). Projected catalog stars are matched by nearest neighbor and accepted using a binomial false-positive probability (tetra3.py:1589).

The output is RA, Dec, roll, FOV, one radial distortion term k (tetra3.py:1641), RMSE, match count and probability, with no WCS or SIP.

It solves in 10–500 ms in Python. Pattern density is uneven across the sky, and limiting the search to the brightest 8 stars fails when bright detections are spurious.

Its catalogs are BSC5, Hipparcos and Tycho (tetra3.py:702-870). Proper motion is applied linearly from 1991.25 to the requested epoch, and stars without proper motion are dropped. It has no UCAC4 or Gaia support.

docs.title: 3.3 cedar-solve (smroid/cedar-solve)
docs.text:
A tetra3 fork with the same API and pixel convention.

Its database, unlike tetra3's, is uniform: patterns are generated in "lattice fields" on a Fibonacci sphere, with a fixed 50 patterns per field, brightest first, in breadth-first combination order (tetra3.py:1182-1308). The table size is the next prime above 3× the pattern count, with linear probing (tetra3.py:1316-1320). Each slot stores a 16-bit key hash, which rejects probe collisions without loading stars (tetra3.py:1382, 2268), plus a float16 longest edge. The magnitude limit is set automatically from the star density needed (tetra3.py:1118-1143). The database is about 38 MB (about 42k stars).

The solve tries every image combination breadth-first, so there is no fixed limit of 8 stars (tetra3.py:1819). Hash bins are visited nearest first (~1855-1866). Match tolerance is 0.002, the default timeout is 5 s, and solves can be canceled. It adds P90E/MAXE errors and the rotation matrix. The distortion range search was removed.

Its catalogs are the same as tetra3's.

There is no Rust solver. smroid's cedar-detect is a Rust star detector:

  • a row gate followed by a 2-D gate, noise estimation, rejection of hot pixels and trails, and 2/4/8× binning;
  • about 10 ms per Mpx on a Raspberry Pi 4;
  • takes 8-bit images only and returns centroids with the first pixel center at 0.5 (src/algorithm.rs:509-528, 958).

It could become the CLI's extractor if it were extended to 16-bit images.

docs.title: 3.4 Comparison
