docs.title: 3.5 What Fayde takes from each
docs.text:
The wider literature (star-tracker identification, robust estimation, distortion fitting, benchmarks) is reviewed in docs/research/literature-review.md. Sections 5, 6 and 9 describe what Fayde implements.

  1. The database layout comes from cedar-solve:
  2. uniform lattice fields with a fixed budget of patterns per field;
  3. brightest-first breadth-first combinations;
  4. a prime-sized table with linear probing;
  5. a 16-bit key check and the longest edge (as f32) in each slot.

A lookup probes every key in the tolerance window (or scans the table when the window holds more keys than the table has slots) and ranks the hits by their exact shape error. The index is a versioned flat binary, read into memory, rather than npz. 2. Verification comes from astrometry.net (Bayesian log-odds with distractors), behind a cheap pre-filter that counts sources landing near catalog stars (§5.4). 3. The output is a real WCS (TAN, with SIP of order 2–3), plus RA, Dec, pixel scale and roll. Fayde fits each seed with an explicit parity and, when the parity is unknown, tries both and verifies each, so the parity is right, which tetra3 does not check. 4. Several indexes for different field widths, like astrometry.net's series, are tried in order of closeness to the frame's diagonal (the widest first when the scale is unknown). A pointing hint rejects a matched pattern with a star farther from the pointing than the search radius plus the frame's half-diagonal. 5. Catalogs are pluggable, and proper motion is applied to every star. Each position moves along its proper motion on the sphere, which holds at the poles, and stars without proper motion are kept with a larger error: all three take shortcuts near the poles or drop such stars.

docs.title: 4. Architecture
docs.text:
Cargo workspace:

fayde/
  crates/
    fayde-core      sky, pixel and epoch types; portable numerical primitives
    fayde-catalog   Catalog trait, UCAC4/Tycho-2/star-table/.fcat readers, proper motion
    fayde-index     HEALPix selection, pattern hash, streamed index file reads and writes
    fayde-solve     Source, SolveRequest, Outcome and Solution; search, verification, fits and covariance
    fayde-wcs       TAN/SIP projections, WCS header cards, WCS prediction from pointing and roll
    fayde-fits      FITS images and source lists, header priors, profiles, WCS file output
    fayde-detect    star, trail and streak detection in an image
    fayde-api       request building and the JSON report, shared by the command line and Python
    fayde-cli       `fayde index build`, `fayde index info`, `fayde catalog`, `fayde solve`,
                    `fayde verify`, `fayde refit`, `fayde detect`, `fayde calibrate`, `fayde bench`,
                    `fayde compare`
    fayde-py        PyO3 bindings (general Python API)

The solver uses fayde-core, fayde-catalog, fayde-index and fayde-wcs. FITS, detection and request orchestration sit outside the solver. fayde-api combines those layers for the CLI and Python. The index reader verifies a checksum in one streamed pass, then parses the index into memory in a second pass.

Dependencies kept small: serde and serde_json (reports, profiles), libm (portable math), pyo3 (Python bindings), flate2 (catalog downloads, in pure Rust). FITS reading and writing, the k-d tree and the linear algebra are Fayde's own. No C toolchain at runtime.

docs.title: 5. Solve pipeline
docs.text:
sources + hints
   ├─ validate geometry and options, filter and rank usable centroids (§5.0)
   ├─ plan pair-seed and pattern-hash stages from the hints and indexes (§5.2a)
   ├─ try hypotheses, refit locally, verify, and select the final TAN/SIP fit (§5.3–5.5)
   ├─ try the predicted WCS if the search found no solution and a prediction was supplied (§5.6)
   └─ report the solution, abstention, or error

Search stages share the request's deadline and hypothesis limit. The relaxed-prior pass, when enabled, uses the remaining budget and continues the hypothesis count.

docs.title: 5.0 Xylist validation (fayde-solve)
docs.text:
A source list can come from any detector, so Fayde checks it before solving:

  • Validate the frame dimensions, search priors, and solver policy. The Python adapter also checks that source arrays have equal lengths.
  • Ignore non-finite centroids and centroids outside the frame. Rank the remaining sources by p_star and flux when supplied. With no flux, use p_star and input order.
  • Demote candidates near a better-ranked centroid. Keep truncated sources as match evidence and exclude them from seeding and fitting.

docs.title: 5.1 Catalog layer (fayde-catalog)
docs.text:
The Catalog trait exposes fallible cone search and scans. Queries specify an optional epoch and magnitude limit plus a magnitude band. Catalog stars carry a sky position, identifier, optional magnitude, and position errors.

UCAC4 reader:

  • Reads the original zone files in place, seeking to the record ranges for each cone. There are 900 zones (z001–z900), each a 0.2° Dec band starting at −90° and sorted by RA, about 113M stars and 8.9 GB in total.
  • Each record is 78 bytes, little-endian, decoded with explicit little-endian conversion (the field layout matches catalogs/ucac4.c:51-119 in astrometry.net):
  • ra u32 (mas) and spd u32 (mas from the south pole, so Dec = spd − 90°);
  • magm/maga i16 (mmag), sigra/sigdc i8 (+128 mas);
  • pmrac/pmdc i16 (0.1 mas/yr, where pmRA already includes cos δ), sigpmr/sigpmd i8 (+128);
  • 2MASS J/H/K, APASS B/V/g/r/i, and rnm u32 (the unique star ID).
  • Two values are sentinels: a magnitude of 20000 means missing, and a proper motion of 32767 means the real value is in u4i/u4hpm.dat, which is loaded once.
  • u4i/u4index.unf holds, for each of the 900 zones × 1440 RA bins (0.25° each), a start offset and a count, so a cone search seeks straight to the rows it needs. The file is optional: a zone file is in RA order, so without it the same rows are found by binary search of the zone file.
  • Positions are ICRS mean positions at epoch 2000.0. cepra/cepdc are central epochs, not the reference epoch: positions do not move from them, but position errors grow from them. Proper motion moves each position to the query epoch as a unit vector on the sphere, the zero-parallax, zero-radial-velocity case of Butkevich & Lindegren (2014), which holds at the poles. The error on each axis grows as √(σ₀² + (t − t_c)²·σμ²) from the central epoch t_c. Stars without valid proper motion keep their 2000.0 position with an inflated position error, rather than being dropped as tetra3 does.
  • The magnitude band is magm (579–642 nm, close to unfiltered silicon) by default, falling back to maga. This is the same default rule as the independent reader behind the test oracle, so results can be compared row for row.
  • UCAC4 is saturated or incomplete brighter than about mag 7–8. A Tycho-2 index covers the bright stars for wide fields.

Test vectors come from an independent UCAC4 reader (crates/fayde-catalog/tests/reader_oracle.rs).

docs.title: 5.2 Index (fayde-index)
docs.text:
Each scale band is built offline from a Catalog and stored in one .fidx file:

  • Stars are selected in HEALPix cells at the index epoch. Each cell keeps its K brightest stars, in a streaming pass, with a minimum separation between stars (default 10″, min_sep_arcsec). A nearby kept star, including across HEALPix boundaries, rejects the candidate unless the candidate is brighter (ties by catalog ID); a better candidate replaces all its fainter neighbors. Rejected stars are not buffered for reconsideration, so results are deterministic for a given catalog stream. This follows astrometry.net's uniformize-catalog approach. It keeps the density even, so the galactic plane does not swamp the hash table and the poles are not empty. The magnitude limit is optional (--mag-limit); stars without a magnitude are left out.
  • Each index is built for one field width (--fov). A solve can load several, tried in order of closeness to the frame's diagonal (the widest first when the scale is unknown, §5.3); index-set.md lists a recommended set.
  • The pattern hash table follows cedar-solve's design:
  • lattice fields with a fixed number of patterns per field, chosen brightest first in breadth-first combination order;
  • the key is 5 sorted edge ratios, binned;
  • the table size is a prime above 3× the pattern count, with linear probing;
  • each slot holds a 16-bit key check, a 32-bit floating-point longest edge, and four star indices.
  • lookup visits neighboring keys or checks stored patterns directly when there are fewer table slots than keys to visit. Candidates are ranked by exact ratio error.
  • Measured on a regional UCAC4 index at 0.4° FOV, 0 of 70 image 4-sets were in the index with 2× lattice oversampling; 30× found 11, 100× (cedar-solve's value) found 35, and the true match always ranked first. Patterns grow roughly linearly with oversampling (431 → 11,645 for the region), so an all-sky index for a sub-degree FOV at 100× is large (rough estimate: tens of millions of patterns, gigabytes). This is a reason hinted solves should start from pair seeds built at solve time (§5.3), with the stored pattern index reserved for loose priors and blind solving.
  • The index has two tiers. The first all-sky benchmark solved 89/100 frames blind with no wrong solutions, but every failure was a dense field whose true patterns were absent from the table (0 of 126–1001 true 4-star sets of the frame's top index stars). There were about 40 index stars per field of view, but patterns were built from each field's 10 brightest, so a frame's brightest stars rarely formed a stored pattern. Fayde therefore uses tetra3/cedar-solve's two densities: the dense tier (20 stars per field of view by default) feeds the pattern-seed pre-filter, and patterns come only from a sparse pattern tier.

The v2 selection, one star per cell of side fov/√10 rounded down to a HEALPix level, put both tiers on nside 256, so half the index became pattern stars and fields were truncated again (6 failures in 149 frames, from 8). The v3 selection kept k brightest stars per coarse HEALPix cell, creating boundary artifacts: a bright star could lose its slot while a nearby, much fainter star in the next cell was promoted.

The v4 selection, which Fayde uses, visits dense-tier stars brightest-first (ties by catalog ID) and accepts each only if no accepted pattern star is within r_min = 0.6 × fov / sqrt(N), with N = pattern_stars_per_fov (default 20). This is ESA tetra3's minimum-separation thinning (Brown & Stubis 2017 / TETRA): the characteristic spacing fov/√N sets an approximate density N/fov², or roughly 10 pattern stars in a square frame whose diagonal is fov. The 0.6 factor is empirical; achieved density depends on the available dense stars, and sparse catalogs can undershoot the target. An incremental Cartesian unit-vector grid checks 27 neighboring buckets with exact chord distances, avoiding cell-boundary and polar artifacts; the existing static k-d tree then supplies lattice-field neighbors. Progress reports the number of pattern stars per fov² over the requested region (or all sky). Pattern membership is stored per star, and the index file format stays v2: v4 names the selection method, not the file format.

On a synthetic uniform all-sky input of 1.6 million dense stars at fov = 1°, v4 retained 751,083 pattern stars, 18.207 per fov² (−9.0% from target 20), in about 1.8–1.9 s for sorting and thinning in release mode. An independent k-d-tree check verifies separation for every retained star. The coarse-boundary and 3″-double regression tests, which failed before v4, pass with it. Regional UCAC4 validation retains 67 dense stars and 9,411 patterns; 5/70 image patterns are present, all ranked first. These v4 results are separate from the oversampling measurements above. - astrometry.net's quad kd-tree (4-D quad codes for blind solving, code tolerance about 0.01) was considered and not adopted (§5.3). - The index is built at a fixed epoch (2025.0 by default; see §10). Stars whose proper motion would move them more than half the pattern tolerance at half the field width in 25 years (about 180 mas/yr per degree of field) are left out of the index, so it stays valid for decades; a star with no proper motion counts as still. Pair seeds, verification and fitting do not use index positions: they read catalog stars propagated to the observation epoch at query time (§5.1), so they still see those stars. UCAC4 propagation errors at epoch 2026 are about 0.06–0.3″ (0.02–0.1 px at 3″/px); Gaia matters only for accuracy goals finer than that. - The header records catalog ID, epoch, magnitude limit, cell level and build parameters, and a trailer holds a content hash. A pattern-hash solution names its index's hash, and the report lists the hash of every index loaded.

docs.title: 5.2a Adaptive search plan
docs.text:
Fayde's default entry point, solve_auto, plans the search from the metadata the request carries instead of defaulting to a blind search. Stages run in order and share one hypothesis count, so the false-alarm accounting covers the whole search. Each solution and each abstention returns the executed plan (search: stage, hypotheses, seconds).

Metadata Stages Pointing + tight scale (σ/scale ≤ 3%) Pair seeds within 3σ of the pointing, when 3σ is at most half the hard radius → pair seeds in the whole prior cone → pattern hash in an inner ring (2σ) → pattern hash to the hard radius Pointing, loose or no scale Pattern hash, inner ring → hard radius (scale-pruned when a scale prior exists) Scale only Pattern hash over the whole index, scale-pruned Nothing Blind: pattern hash over every index band search_outside_pointing (opt-in) After the above, pattern hash outside the pointing limit; the solution is flagged prior_violated

The pair seeds look close to the pointing first when its σ is small. The work of a pair-seed stage grows with the area of its cone, and a pipeline's pointing is often far better than the hard limit it is willing to set: measured on 146 real source lists, the pointing was within 2.7′ while the limit was 2°, and a solve cost 8.7 ms at the 2° limit against 1.1 ms at 0.25°. The first look is skipped when 3σ is more than half the hard radius, which includes the default σ of a quarter of it: a first look nearly as wide as the limit costs almost as much as the search it would spare. The σ comes from the request (--pointing-sigma) or the instrument profile, which fayde calibrate fills in from solved frames.

With a pointing and a tight scale the pair seeds go first even when an index is loaded. The reverse was tried: one hash stage ahead of the pair seeds halves the median solve on real source lists, but with an all-sky index a stage that finds nothing costs 37 to 395 ms, against 3 ms for the pair-seed solve it delays, and the mean went from 4.5 ms to 24 ms (docs/references.md, "Considered and not adopted").

The inner ring is skipped when 2σ ≥ 0.8 × hard radius (the second pass would add nothing). Indexes whose region cannot contain the field are skipped, and implausible priors are rejected rather than searched: a scale prior that implies a field wider than a hemisphere (header placeholders such as CDELT = 1) is an input error, and fayde-fits drops such header scales with a warning. A sequence stage (predict from the previous frame, §5.6) will go first once implemented.

docs.title: 5.3 Matchers (fayde-solve)
docs.text:
• Image sources are tried in order of p_star × brightness, not brightness alone, widening the set progressively (PROSAC; Chum & Matas 2005). In frames tracking satellites, the brightest detections are often not stars.
  • With a pointing hint and a tight scale prior, the matcher uses pair seeds (k-vector; Mortari). It fetches the brightest catalog stars in the hint cone at solve time and builds a list of their pair separations. The fainter stars that a hypothesis is verified against are read around the hypotheses that pass the pre-filter, not for the whole cone, which is tens of frame areas. Each image pair from the top of the source order is looked up by separation (tolerance from the scale σ and position errors). One matched pair and a choice of parity fix rotation, scale and translation. The roll prior can rule out a seed. With half the sources false, a pair is all-real 25% of the time and a 4-star pattern only 6%.
  • With a pointing hint and a loose scale prior, the matcher uses the pattern hash. It builds patterns from the ordered image sources and looks up only hash entries whose stars lie in the cone. The scale range prunes by edge length before lookup.
  • Fayde has no geometric-voting fallback (Kolomenkin et al. 2008), in which image pairs vote for catalog pairs of matching separation. A source list dominated by false detections can use up the search budget before a seed finds real stars.
  • A blind solve does pattern-hash lookups across the indexes loaded, each built for one field width (as astrometry.net's index series), the closest to the frame's diagonal first (the widest when the scale is unknown), with hypotheses counted across all of them. astrometry.net's 4-D quad codes were considered and not adopted: the 5 edge ratios describe the same four-point shape, and the hash lookup already gives continuous-tolerance matching (docs/references.md, "Considered and not adopted").
  • Each stage tries candidate transforms in deterministic order. The search returns a hypothesis once it passes verification and the final fit.

docs.title: 5.4 Verifier
docs.text:
The pre-filter projects the first 12 ranked sources outside the seed and counts those that land within 3σ + 2 px + 0.01·d of a star, d being the distance in pixels from the seed's center: at least 2 among the catalog stars read for pair seeds, at least 1 among the index's stars for pattern seeds. Hypotheses that pass go on to the full test.

A seed transform from 2–4 stars is rough, so the hypothesis is refitted on its provisional inliers (weighted, §5.5), re-matched, and only then scored (LO-RANSAC; Chum, Matas & Kittler 2003). This rescues correct hypotheses whose seed transform was slightly off.

The full test is Bayesian log-odds as in astrometry.net (solver/verify.c:448-620, distractor ratio 0.25 by default): for each image source in rank order (§5.0), the probability it matches a projected catalog star (Gaussian with the combined position error) versus being a distractor (uniform over the field). The default acceptance threshold is ln(10⁹) after the hypothesis-count correction. Fayde combines the centroid error (sigma_px or the policy default) with catalog uncertainty, uses p_star to adjust the distractor probability, and stretches the match gate along a known trail for truncated sources. The solve also scores its pointing, roll and scale priors. The verifier treats each position error as isotropic and doesn't compare brightnesses.

Each solution reports its number of false alarms (NFA), hypotheses_tested × exp(−log_odds). Acceptance uses the log-odds minus the natural logarithm of the hypothesis count. The fixed-model likelihood argument assumes independent uniform null sources. Refitting on provisional matches uses some of the scored sources to select the model. End-to-end false-accept rates therefore need empirical calibration for each search regime (§9).

docs.title: 5.5 Fit (fayde-solve)
docs.text:
• Seed transforms use the supplied parity or try both image parities.
  • The weighted least-squares TAN fit uses the centroid and catalog position error at the observation epoch.
  • The robust fit is iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) over the same Gaussian-plus-distractor mixture the verifier uses. Each match gets a soft weight from its probability of being real; there is no hard kσ clipping. The fit and the verifier therefore agree on what an outlier is.
  • A global error-scale factor s on the supplied covariances is fitted and reported. s ≫ 1 means the producer under-reports its centroid errors, which is useful feedback to detector authors.
  • Fayde fits SIP distortion per frame, with the order chosen by BIC. Fayde doesn't fit one distortion model across many frames, as a SCAMP-style global solution does (Bernstein et al. 2017). Among orders up to BIC's choice, the lowest whose weighted mean squared error on held-out cells of the frame is within 5% of the best is kept (with matches in fewer than four of the nine cells, no distortion; when the order cannot be scored, BIC's choice stands). SIP is also dropped, or the hypothesis rejected, when a cell of a 3 × 3 grid with at least 6 sources has confident matches at under a quarter of the frame's rate. When the request has a scale or roll prior, a solution with distortion is converged again as TAN with scale and roll free of the priors: a TAN outside the hint's limits that explains the sources at least as well replaces it and is then refused, and a TAN inside them replaces it only with higher posterior odds. Distortion must not stand in for a scale or roll the hint held back.
  • The solution carries CRVAL, CRPIX at image center, CD, optional SIP, parameter covariance, per-star residuals, weighted RMS, and a leave-one-out RMS when there are enough matches.

docs.title: 5.6 Sequence mode
docs.text: The solver keeps state for a sequence ID: last WCS, timestamps, fitted pointing drift. For frame N it predicts the WCS, runs §5.4 only, and accepts if it passes. This replaces a pipeline-side neighbor-hint ladder for the common case and stays separate from WCS borrowing: Fayde never returns a WCS that did not pass verification on the frame itself.

docs.title: 6. Input contract
docs.text: The Rust request types define what the solver consumes. The shared API resolves header values, instrument profiles and caller overrides before building that request. See the FITS source-list format for the file contract.

docs.title: 6.1 Principles
docs.text: Give Fayde the frame dimensions, source centroids, and any measured centroid errors, fluxes, and star probabilities. Supply uncertainty with a pointing, scale, or roll estimate so the search can rank hypotheses and apply the intended limits. Fayde records where each prior came from in the CLI and Python reports.

docs.title: 6.2 Frame
docs.text: Field Input width, height Image dimensions in pixels. Supply them directly, through the image, or through the source list and its header. trail Optional common star trail. The Rust request takes full length in pixels and angle in radians from +x toward +y. The CLI, Python options and FITS source list take degrees. Observation epoch Set Policy::epoch in Rust or use an epoch override or observation header in the CLI and Python. Without one, file-backed catalogs use J2000.0, and the CLI and Python warn.

docs.title: 6.3 Sources
docs.text:
Source field Meaning x, y Centroid in pixels. Rust and Python default to zero-based pixel centers. FITS source-list positions are one-based. flux Optional integrated flux in linear units, used for ranking. sigma_px Optional isotropic 1σ centroid error in pixels. The policy supplies the default. p_star Optional probability that a detection is a star, from 0 to 1. truncated Whether the frame edge or a mask cuts the source. Fayde uses truncated sources to score a match and excludes them from seeding and fitting. A known trail widens the match gate along its direction.

The solver ranks centroids itself. Keep uncertain candidates with a low p_star when the upstream detector can estimate one. The verifier takes one isotropic position error per source, and it doesn't compare source brightness with catalog magnitudes.

docs.title: 6.3a Frame-level detector outputs
docs.text: The detection report contains its mode, background and noise estimates, and per-source measurements. In straight-trail mode, the common length and angle accompany the source list. For a source measured along and across a trail, the solver receives the larger position error as sigma_px. See Read the detection report.

docs.title: 6.4 Priors
docs.text: Input Effect Pointing center, 1σ error and maximum radius Set the search region and contribute to the score. Scale in arcsec/px and 1σ error Select index bands and prune hypotheses. A tight scale and pointing enable pair-seed search. Roll, 1σ error and maximum deviation Constrain image orientation. Parity Choose the image handedness.

docs.title: 6.5 Instrument model
docs.text: The JSON instrument profile can supply a scale and its uncertainty, binning, parity, a roll rule based on a header keyword, pointing uncertainty and radius, and whether to use the frame's WCS as a hint. Caller overrides take precedence, followed by the profile and then the image header. Detection can also use the profile's charge-transfer and periodic-background corrections. See the instrument profile example and the calibration guide.

docs.title: 6.6 Observer
docs.text: Fayde doesn't model the observer. It applies no stellar aberration from the observer's velocity, no light-time correction and no refraction, and it computes no observer state from a TLE or a ground site. Fayde solves each frame on its own: a solved neighbor's WCS can seed the next frame (§5.6), but Fayde keeps no state across a sequence and never interpolates a WCS between frames.

docs.title: 6.7 Solve policy
docs.text: Field Default Effect deadline None Starts when the solver receives the request. An accepted hypothesis can finish its final fit. max_hypotheses 5,000,000 Limits scored hypotheses across the search stages. accept_log_odds ln(10⁹) Threshold after subtracting the log of the hypothesis count. default_sigma_px 1 px Position error for a source without sigma_px. max_sip_order 3 Upper limit for SIP model selection. epoch None: J2000.0 for file-backed catalogs Target epoch for catalog proper motion.

docs.title: 6.8 Encodings
docs.text:
• In Rust, construct SolveRequest with frame, sources, priors, policy, and previous. Pass the catalog and any indexes to the solver. fayde_api::build_request can resolve the header and profile first.
  • In Python, use Solver.solve with coordinate sequences, Solver.solve_image with a FITS path, NumPy array or Astropy HDU, or Solver.solve_detection with a detection report. Header cards or a keyword dictionary provide frame metadata.
  • On the command line, use fayde solve --image with a FITS image or fayde solve --sources with a FITS binary table. Add --header, --instrument, or explicit options as needed.

docs.title: 6.9 Integrating with a host pipeline
docs.text:
1. Send the detector's source list and the frame header, or pass the image to Fayde's detector.
  2. Supply a catalog path and any indexes needed for the search. In Python, reuse one Solver across frames so it opens them once.
  3. Read the solution or abstention before using the WCS. A solved report includes WCS cards, matched pairs and residuals, uncertainty estimates, and the catalog and index identity. The Rust solution also exposes the parameter covariance.
  4. Compare solutions against the host's current backend on the same frames. Measure solve rate, residuals, and latency before switching the default.

docs.title: 7. Error handling
docs.text:
• An exhausted search returns Outcome::Abstained with its reason, best log-odds if available, hypothesis count, and search trace.
  • Errors are for bad input (non-finite hints, zero image size) and unreadable index/catalog.
  • A hypothesis limit or deadline that runs out also returns Outcome::Abstained, with that reason, the best log-odds seen (no WCS), the hypothesis count and the trace.

docs.title: 8. Licensing
docs.text:
Fayde is GPL-3.0-or-later from 0.3.3 (LICENSE, NOTICE); 0.3.0 to 0.3.2 were Apache-2.0.

  • tetra3 and cedar-solve (Apache-2.0): code may be ported with notices kept.
  • astrometry.net: mostly BSD-3, which is compatible with notices kept. Some components are GPL. Fayde takes no code from them: code under another author's copyleft license would stop the copyright holder from relicensing Fayde. Rule: port from papers (Lang et al. 2010) and BSD files only; check the license header of every file before porting from it.
  • Catalog data: Fayde's releases contain no catalog data and no built indexes.

docs.title: 9. Validation
docs.text:
1. Unit tests cover projection round trips, edge-ratio codes, and UCAC4 record decoding against an independent reader on the same zones.
  2. On synthetic data, fayde bench solves source lists projected from the catalog with a known WCS, with position noise, false sources and missing stars, and measures the recovery error. Every other list holds only random positions, to count false solutions.
  3. On real frames, fayde compare checks each solution against a stored reference WCS on a 5 × 5 grid of image points.
  4. As a guard against false positives, fayde bench counts and reports the random lists that solve. Whether the false-accept rate stays within what the reported NFA predicts (§5.4) isn't measured.

Fayde's results haven't been compared with other solvers on shared public frames.

docs.title: 10. Decisions
docs.text:
1. The index is built at a fixed epoch, high-proper-motion stars are excluded from patterns, and positions are propagated rigorously at query time (§5.2).

docs.title: Trails and streaks in one detector
docs.text: This design extends fayde-detect (detection.md) to frames whose stars are trails: a straight-trail pass (§4, measured in §7) and empirical kernels for curved paths (§8). Literature: docs/research/literature-review.md §7.4 and §8. Sources: docs/references.md.

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
One detector, fayde-detect, that takes any frame from an imager pointed at the sky and returns what the solver needs, whatever moved during the exposure:

Frame Stars Other things in it Fayde Sidereal tracking, or a spacecraft holding its attitude points satellite or debris streaks, cosmic-ray tracks handled; streaks only above about 5σ per PSF area Tracking a satellite, a slew, a drift trails, all the same length and direction the tracked object (a point), other satellites (streaks), cosmic rays handled for straight trails at least 7 FWHM long (§7) Either, with a faint satellite as above a streak below the per-pixel noise not found

In trails mode the output adds the frame's star trail with its evidence, point-like sources (among them the tracked object), and per-source errors along and across the trail. The constraints are the point pass's (detection.md §1): no parameter the user must know, the same bits on every machine, no unsafe, no new dependency. Its cost is in §7.

The straight-trail detector fits a common length and direction across the frame. The empirical kernel can measure a shared curved path or field rotation when it learns a reliable template (§8). When Fayde detects trails but cannot establish a consistent model, the report records the reason and the detector uses its point measurements.

docs.title: 2. What exists
docs.text:
The point pass, fayde-detect's pipeline for point sources, applies a Gaussian matched filter of the measured width, estimates the background and noise of the filtered image on a mesh, finds peaks, fits each with a log-quadratic (position, size, axis ratio, direction), and classes them (star, saturated, extended, sharp), then gives each a p_star from its class and its local false discovery rate. Streaks are traced from ridge-like peaks (axis ratio at least twice the stars') along a running least-squares line and reported with their ends; every peak on one is kept out of the star list. A drift that smears every star a little is handled by judging shape against the frame's own stars (detection.md §3.3). 109 of 109 real point-source frames solve, and point-pass detection takes a median 2.2 ms per frame (§7).

An earlier detector, fayde-trails (about 3,100 lines, not merged), had:

  • a line matched filter computed directly (cost proportional to pixels × trail length), with an AVX2 path and a thread pool;
  • a clip loop, min(image, 2 · line mean), iterated so that compact bright sources do not leak into the line response;
  • the frame's trail from the flux-weighted second moments of connected components: L = √(12 · (λmajor − λminor)), direction from the major axis, with a verdict (Trails, Compact, Ambiguous, PriorMismatch, NoGeometry) and an optional prior that selects the population.

On 74 real frames tracking satellites, measured against a reference WCS per frame: with a header prior its source lists solved 74 of 74; without one it refused 2 frames as ambiguous and the other 72 solved. Median center error 0.31 px against 0.50 px for fayde-detect's streak table used as a source list; 25 catalog matches against 16. Those figures predate its change to portable math.

The solver accepts Frame::trail (length, angle). A source flagged truncated counts as evidence with a gate stretched along the trail but is never fitted or used as a seed. The verifier can add a variance along one direction to a gate (verify.rs, an extra term in quadrature). Everything else is isotropic: Source::sigma_px is one number, a match carries one σ, a fitted pair one weight, and the WCS covariance one normal matrix shared by both coordinates (verify.rs, fit.rs). Sources whose position falls outside the image are dropped (solve.rs).

The point pass alone solves 9 of 84 frames tracking satellites (§7), so a second pass is needed. It can't reuse fayde-trails, whose costs (unsafe, a thread pool, cost growing with trail length) conflict with the workspace's rules.

docs.title: 3. What the literature gives
docs.text:
Detail and reading levels in the literature review, §8. The facts this design rests on:

  1. A trail needs its own filter. The matched filter for a trail is the PSF convolved with the segment. Its signal-to-noise ratio over a point filter's tends to √(L / (2√π·σ)) for L ≫ σ (Nir, Zackay & Ofek 2018). The LSST trailing-loss fits (Jones, SMTN-003) agree:
Trail length / FWHM 2 5 10 20 Gain, exact for a Gaussian PSF in white noise (computed) 0.12 mag 0.60 1.00 1.39 Gain, long-trail limit √(L / 1.505 FWHM) 0.15 mag 0.65 1.03 1.40 Gain, from SMTN-003's fits (point a = 0.420, b = 0.003; trail a = 0.761, b = 1.162) 0.18 mag 0.60 0.97 1.34

Below about 2 FWHM the point filter gives up little; that is where the point pass stays. 2. The filter must be aimed. For long trails the matched response falls with an angle error Δθ as (√π / 2z)·erf(z), z = L·|Δθ| / 4σ: 2% lost at Δθ = σ/L, 7.7% at 2σ/L, 25% at 4σ/L. A length off by a factor k keeps 1/√k (a factor of 2 loses 29%, in the long-trail limit; 26% computed at L = 40σ), so lengths are measured, not taken from a coarse grid. (Derived; checked numerically. No published closed form was found.) 3. One trail per frame is cheap to find. The median orientation and major-axis length of bright elongated components gives it, and the median ignores a satellite streak or cosmic rays (Danescu & Turcu 2026: astrometry.net went from 15 to 39 of 40 frames solved once the image was filtered with that trail). The second moments give the length only for whole, evenly lit trails and a round PSF; components cut by the threshold read short. 4. An aimed box costs approximately O(1) per pixel. A running sum along translates of one digital line (Soille, Breen & Jones 1996) costs two additions per pixel whatever the length. It is not translation invariant: the pixels a window covers change with its phase along the digital line, so the effective length and centering depend on the angle. The Gaussian applied after it hides most of that; how much is left has to be measured against a direct filter. 5. The error of a trail is not round. For a Gaussian PSF convolved with a segment (Vereš et al. 2012; erf model as corrected by Bouquillon et al. 2017), when the background dominates, the error along the trail grows as L and across it as √L; when the star dominates, the error across is a static star's and the error along grows as √L (Bouquillon et al. 2017, Cramér–Rao bounds, for the model's own parameters; a fit with more nuisance parameters does worse). A brightness slope along the trail needs a tilt term (Blake et al. 2026); tracking jitter is common to every star in a frame, so an empirical profile stacked from bright trails beats the ideal model (Kouprianov 2008). 6. Faint streaks are found by multiscale line sums. Line integrals at a subsampled set of positions (spacing L/2 along the line), angles and dyadic lengths, built bottom-up (Brandt & Dym 1999; Ofir et al. 2020), about 8N responses per length and O(N log N) in all. For the mean of w·L independent pixels the noise threshold from K tests is σ·√(2 ln(K/δ) / (w·L)) (Ofir et al. 2020). Dyadic lines stray from true lines by up to log₂ n / 6 px for an image side n (Karpenko & Ershov 2021): 1.7 px at n = 1024. 7. One acceptance rule serves every line, as long as every test is counted. The number of false alarms, K · P(noise ≥ observed) (von Gioi et al. 2010 and the a-contrario school; Grosjean & Moisan 2009 for linear filters in Gaussian noise), is a union bound: it needs no independence between tests, but it needs valid null probabilities and every search counted. Clipping, masking, fitted-star subtraction, data-chosen geometry and endpoint optimization all change the null, so a whole pipeline has to be calibrated on simulated frames, not only the formula. 8. Point against segment is not a regular test. Length 0 is on the boundary of the parameter space and the angle is undefined under it (Self & Liang 1987; Davies 1987). Wilks's χ² and the usual BIC approximation do not apply; penalties calibrated by simulation do. 9. Others found these vetoes useful: a streak as wide as the PSF (narrower is likely a cosmic ray: Bektešević & Vinković 2017); the response across against along (Han et al. 2025); a centroid that moves when the model is fitted means a blend (Blake et al. 2026); a trail within L/2 of the edge is cut (Sharma et al. 2023 discard it; §4.6 uses it).

docs.title: 4. Method
docs.text:
image
  │ A. point pass (unchanged): filter, mesh, peaks, fits, classes, bright streaks
  │ B. trail census: one straight star trail common to the frame? → points | trails | refused
  │ C. segment pass (trails mode): masks, aimed segment filter, seeds
  │ D. one fit per trail on raw pixels: shared length, angle, width; position, flux, background free
  │ E. classes from a trail model and a point model: star, point, sharp
  ▼
stars (x, y, σ, σ along, σ across, flux, p_star) + streaks + point-like sources + frame trail

The trail pass runs unless it is turned off (--no-trails). When the point pass binned the image, B uses a full-resolution point pass, saved before binning or run again. A frame that ends as points or refused keeps the point pass's star list bit for bit (the test point_frames_are_untouched in crates/fayde-detect/tests/trails.rs). An empirical kernel (§8) can still take a frame over: a field-rotation kernel after a points census, a shared curved template after a refusal, or over an accepted straight trail under the stronger conditions in §8. The frame's mode is then kernel.

docs.title: 4.1 Trail census (B)
docs.text:
Two estimates that fail in different ways; trails mode only when they agree.

  1. The first estimate comes from shapes. The filtered image is cut into 8-connected components of pixels above 4σ. A component votes when its peak is not masked and is at least 6σ, its variance ratio is at least 2.25 and it is at least 3 px long. Its vote is its direction and L = √(12·(λmajor − λminor)), weighted by its peak signal-to-noise ratio capped at 30, so one bright satellite cannot outvote fifty stars. The votes go into a circular histogram of the axis (an axis has no sign) in 36 bins of 5°, smoothed with weights 1, 2, 1. The largest mode gives θ₁, the weighted mean axis of the votes within 12.5° of it. A second mode more than 15° away, with at least 5 votes and half the first mode's weight, is a second population. L₁ is the weighted median length of the mode's votes whose peaks reach 18σ with no saturated pixel, or of all the mode's votes when fewer than 3 do. Taking the median length of the components follows Danescu & Turcu 2026 and fayde-trails; the weights and the 18σ choice are Fayde's. Components within 2 px of the edge do not vote for the length.
  2. The second comes from pixel pairs: the autocovariance of the filtered image. Unmasked pixels above 3σ serve as anchors; at least 50 are needed, and large sets are thinned to about 5,000. Each partner counts as the ratio of its signal-to-noise ratio to its anchor's, at most 2, and a masked partner counts as 0. Masked are the frame's mask, a zone around traced streaks that are not star trails, and pixels at 0.8 of saturation or more, grown by 3 px. The direction θ₂ is found coarse to fine: 36 directions at a lag of four trail widths (less for short trails), refined with a parabola, then the lag doubled up to L₁/2 with 17 angles a quarter of a width apart at that lag. A field of identical trails gives an elongated central peak; along θ₂ its profile is a triangle of half-width L blurred by a Gaussian of √2·σₜ (σₜ the trail width with the filter's), plus a near-flat floor from the pairs of different stars. L₂ is the L of the best fit of that model (amplitude and floor fitted linearly for each trial L from L₁/2 to 2L₁ in steps of 0.25 px), not where the profile reaches the floor.

The decision (census.reason in the report says which rule decided):

Outcome Rule points No vote; fewer than 5 votes in the mode; under half the weight in the mode (without a prior); elongated components carrying under 5% of the capped weight of all bright components; or L₁ under 7 FWHM across the trail (real frames meant to show points drift by up to 6.8 FWHM, §7) trails θ₁ and θ₂ within max(3σₜ/L₁, 0.08 rad), lengths within 20%, the straightness check passes, and the refit below accepts the geometry refused Two populations; the estimates disagree; the trails change across the frame; trails longer than the frame (no length votes, or fewer than 3 whole trails while at least 75% of the votes touch the edge); more than four round sources of the stars' width per trail vote; fewer than 50 anchors, or no fit of the second estimate with a positive amplitude; or the refit rejects the geometry

The straightness check cuts the frame into 3 × 3 regions. A region with at least 4 votes gives an angle, and with at least 5 whole, unsaturated votes reaching 18σ a length. The frame is refused when a region's angle is off by more than twice the angle tolerance, or its length by more than 50%. With fewer than 2 regions measured, Fayde refuses the frame if fewer than 3 trails fit, or if the spread of their fitted angles exceeds max(2w/L, 0.05) rad.

In the refit, the frame's length, angle and width are the medians of up to 15 of the brightest isolated whole trails, each fitted with all three free (at most 30 steps, χ²/dof at most 4); the census's values stand when none settles. When at least 3 fits, and over half of all attempts, come out more than 20% shorter than both the census length and their components' lengths, the geometry is rejected: such fits follow part of a curve.

When radiation hits crowd the frame, or no trail emerges while at least 5 bright components are long and narrow (axis ratio 4 or more), the census is retried once on a cleaned image, with only its anchors and votes changed (§7 lists the cleaning steps).

An angle prior (--trail-angle, Python trail_angle) selects a mode within 15° of it and then waives the share and second-population rules; the geometry is still measured from the image, as in fayde-trails. Detection takes no length, and no prior from the instrument profile or the header. In refused, the point-pass star list is returned. The report's census holds both estimates, the vote counts and shares, the elongated share, and the number of regions with their worst angle and length deviations; trail holds the refined geometry with its errors.

docs.title: 4.2 Segment pass (C)
docs.text:
1. A point convolved with a segment kernel is a segment-shaped response, so every hot pixel and cosmic-ray hit would become a faint false trail. The filter's input is masked, set to zero on the point pass's sharp detections and cosmic-ray tracks (when it ran at full resolution), pixels that are sharp at full resolution (sharp_in_raw) and undefined pixels. Saturated pixels stay in the filter and are left out of the fits. Traced streaks that are not star trails are subtracted with an erf model first. The raw image is kept for the fit (D).
  2. The aimed filter is a running sum along lines at θ, taken on sheared rows and interpolated between rows, with fractional ends weighted, so that its length is the physical L at every angle (the running box of Soille, Breen & Jones 1996 uses digital lines instead). Then a Gaussian of the trail's width (σ between 0.6 and 4 px). A unit test checks the box against sums along the line.
  3. For a smooth stationary Gaussian field of unit variance, the density of maxima above a high level u tends to (√det Λ / 2π)·u·φ(u), where Λ is the covariance of the field's gradient (Adler & Taylor 2007). The point pass's threshold is the smaller of that bound for a Gaussian kernel and the pixel tail. For the aimed filter, Λ comes from the model profiles along and across the trail, sampled every 0.25 px; along a long trail it scales as 1/(√π·σ·L). On frames whose sky is clipped at a floor the automatic threshold is at least 5σ. The bound is checked on empty frames for the point pass only.
  4. Filtering a trail with a box of its own length gives a blurred triangular response along the trail with its maximum at the trail's center, so each maximum is a seed near the center. A maximum within L/2 along the trail and 1.5 filter widths across of a brighter one is dropped; at most 5,000 seeds are kept.
  5. The mesh measures noise from differences of pixel pairs set apart (mesh.rs). In trails mode the pairs are set more than a trail apart (L + 3σk for the filtered image, L + 6w for the fit's weights), so that two pixels of one trail are not paired and the noise is not underestimated.

docs.title: 4.3 One fit per trail (D)
docs.text:
1. The model is an erf along the trail (Bouquillon et al. 2017) times a Gaussian across, of variance w² + 1/12 for the pixel's width, evaluated at pixel centers on the raw image. The frame's L, θ and width are fixed; position, flux and a background plane (a gradient, for stray light) are free. Weights are 1 / (σ² + s / gain), with σ the mesh's sky noise and s the model's signal above the background plus any subtracted neighbor or streak light (the photon term only when the gain is known), recomputed at each step. On frames whose sky is clipped at a floor, a prior holds the background.
  2. The fit starts from the center of light along the line (halfway there on clipped-sky frames) and the seed's position across it. A fit that moves more than 1 px is started once more from where it ended.
  3. The fit takes at most 8 bounded Gauss–Newton steps (24 on clipped-sky frames). A step is capped at max(0.1·L, 1) px, and a step that reverses is halved. The fit converges when its step is under a tenth of the position error (between 0.001 and 0.05 px) and counts when it is under half. A fit that leaves its stamp, cannot be solved or does not settle is dropped, and so is a trail known no better than half a trail along (one FWHM on clipped-sky frames) or two widths across, or a point known no better than two widths either way. Fixed limits keep the work and the bits fixed.
  4. The errors come from the inverse normal matrix at the parameters returned; they are projected along and across the trail (σ_along, σ_across) and floored. An optional test (error_claims_cover_the_truth) checks them on simulated frames: for matched stars away from the edge, 58 to 78% of the residuals within 1σ and at least 86% within 2σ, on each axis.
  5. Fits that converge within 1.5 widths of each other are merged when both fit well (χ²/dof at most 2). The others are fitted again with their neighbors' models subtracted where their light reaches the stamp; the first fit stays if the second fails.

docs.title: 4.4 Classes (E)
docs.text:
Each seed is fitted as a trail. It is also fitted as a point (the PSF, L = 0) when 40% of its light along the line lies within 2w + 1 px of its brightest column, or its trail fit has χ²/dof above 2. The two are compared on a common stamp centered on the fitted trail:

Model Free Class (morphology) To the solver Star trail: the frame's L, θ, width position, flux, background star yes Point: the PSF position, flux, background point no; reported Point narrower than a star can be sharp no

With d = ½(χ²point − χ²trail) on that stamp, the trail's probability against a point is p_trail = 1 / (1 + e^(−d)) (equal priors): a seed with p_trail of at least 0.5 is a star, otherwise a point. A point whose brightest pixel, less 3σ, holds more than 2.5 times the share of light a star puts in its brightest pixel is sharp (a hot pixel or a cosmic ray). p_star is (1 − local false discovery rate) × p_trail. Likelihood ratios between these models do not follow χ² (§3, item 8), so p_trail is a relative weight, not a calibrated probability.

The classes describe shape, not what the object is: a point in a trailed frame is often the tracked object but can be anything moving with it. A cosmic-ray track that lies along the trail can pass as a star.

docs.title: 4.5 Streaks
docs.text: The point pass traces streaks before the census, with no trail direction: its seeds are peaks elongated at least twice as much as the stars. After the census, a traced streak is removed with its sources when it looks like a star trail (within 3·max(2w/L, 0.05) rad of the trail, at most 3 trails long, not a cosmic ray) or a chain of star trails (within 12° and uneven along its length); the aimed filter's seeds then measure that light. Other streaks are subtracted before the trail pass, and a seed on one is kept only if its fit has χ²/dof of at most 1.5.

docs.title: 4.6 Trails cut by the edge
docs.text:
A trail whose outer end lies beyond the edge has a centroid biased by up to L/2 along it when it is measured as a blob. The fit holds the frame's L and θ fixed and fits the visible pixels, so it places a cut trail's center where the whole trail's would be, which can fall outside the image (on clipped-sky frames such sources are dropped). A trail is flagged truncated when its center is closer to an edge than half the trail's length projected toward that edge plus two widths. The solver scores a truncated source with a gate stretched along the trail but neither seeds nor fits with it, and drops a source whose center is outside the image (§2).

On a square frame whose trails are a tenth of its width, about one star in eight is cut (12.4% averaged over directions, 10 to 13.6% depending on the direction).

New public fields in fayde-detect, fayde-api and fayde-fits break Rust code that builds those structs with a literal, and an exhaustive match on Class must handle Point

docs.title: 6. Integration choices and prior art
docs.text: Most of this is known technique put together: a segment-shaped PSF fitted with its neighbors' models subtracted is PSF photometry (Stetson 1987) with a longer PSF, and Houtz & Frueh 2021 and Sharma et al. 2023 already detect trails before plate solving. For one part, the survey (§8 of the literature review) found no antecedent, though that doesn't show none exists: the census's refusal rule, a segmentation-based estimate checked against a segmentation-free one, with regional straightness, and no trails mode unless they agree.

Results on real frames (one laptop core, an instrument profile for the camera, UCAC4 with its index, the frame's header pointing):

Point pass only With the trail pass 109 frames whose stars are points: star lists identical to the point pass's 109 of 109 Detection time, median, those frames 2.2 ms 3.0 ms 84 frames tracking satellites, trails 9 to 85 px (header rate × exposure): solved 9 66 Of those, in trails mode 58, all solved Detection time, median, trails mode 40 ms Median residual of the solutions, trailed frames solved 1.6 px (9 frames) 1.64 px (66 frames)

No frame that the point pass alone solves is lost.

The design has these limits:

  • Cost: trails mode takes a median 40 ms per frame, against 2.2 ms for the point pass alone and 3.0 ms with the census on point-source frames. The fits are most of it.
  • 26 of the 84 frames are not in trails mode (14 called points, most with trails under 20 px; 12 refused, mostly because the two estimates disagree on real trails, whose brightness is not uniform along them), and 18 stay unsolved. The census also misses faint long trails: a 160 px trail spreads a star's light so thin that it may not stand out in the point filter the census votes from.
  • The census refuses two trail populations of comparable weight unless an angle prior selects one, and refuses the geometry when too few trails have both ends in the frame.
  • For straight trails, the solver gets one isotropic error per source, the larger of the errors along and across the trail, so the error across the trail is overstated.
  • A cut trail's error is the fit's own: the error of the frame's shared length and angle is not carried as one term common to every cut trail. On real frames, 411 cut trails had a spread along the trail of 1.65 times the claimed error, against 1.25 for whole trails.
  • Trails that nearly coincide are not split by a joint fit. Where fitted neighbors overlap, a seed is fitted again with their models subtracted; the first fit stays if the second fails.
  • The straight-trail fit has no term for brightness that changes along the trail.
  • Streaks fainter than about 5σ per PSF area are not found.

docs.title: 8. Empirical kernels for curved star paths
docs.text: Tracking, rolling, or wobbling during an exposure can spread each star along a curve. A straight-trail filter can lock onto fragments of the path, giving the solver too few stars and positions displaced from their exposure-averaged coordinates.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Training reuses the census components and the census's defect mask. For a shared path, it keeps up to 64 bright, isolated, unsaturated components away from the frame edge, with lengths and orientations in the dominant mode. Their cutouts are background-subtracted with the mesh, normalized by flux and registered by their centers of light, then aligned twice to the current mean using subpixel correlation peaks. The template is their clipped, noise-weighted mean, recentered on its own light. This empirical PSF follows the approach of DAOPHOT and PSFEx. Its origin represents the exposure-averaged position of the star.
  2. When the straight-trail census accepts or refuses a dominant trail, Fayde measures the template's center of light in 2 px slices along its major axis and uses the empirical template when the path's RMS deviation from the best straight line is at least 0.5 px. When the census has already accepted one straight trail, the template overrides it only if it stacks at least 15 stars and bends by at least 1 px. On real frames tracking satellites, templates of 6 to 11 stars bent by 0.6 to 3 px moved solutions by up to 1.7 px from the straight-trail fits, which agreed with Gaia to 0.05–0.1 px. Every template must stack at least 10 stars: its center of light is every position's origin, so its error moves the whole solution (a template of 5 stars on a sparse simulated frame put the solution 2.6 px off). The sum of distances between slices estimates the path length. Evidence of field rotation can also select kernel mode when the census finds no common direction.
  3. The background-subtracted full-resolution image is correlated with the taps that hold 99% of the template's light. Undefined pixels, hot pixels, and cosmic-ray hits are masked with the trail pass's mask. Peaks are found with the mesh and the point pass's peak finder, using an equivalent Gaussian scale from the template's gradient covariance, and are visited in descending correlation amplitude.
  4. Each fit starts from a quadratic peak interpolation and refines the position and flux against the template in the image. The fitted signal must clear the noise threshold and agree with the template across its support. Each accepted source is subtracted in image space. Testing the correlation on the residual image applies the predicted autocorrelation of every brighter source with its actual subpixel shift and mask, which suppresses its sidelobes. A second correlation pass recovers peaks that were hidden by bright neighbors. This is a bounded, CLEAN-style subtraction.
  5. The flux is the matched-filter amplitude, and the position errors come from the template's gradient Fisher matrix. The weights include photon noise when the gain is available and an allowance for template mismatch. Each source's p_star comes from the local false discovery rate. The report gives the template size, training count, path length, bend, and region count. An image solve that abstains with time and hypotheses left retries with point detections.

docs.title: Field rotation and limits
docs.text:
For small field rotations, elongated components trace tangents to circles about a common center. The center is fitted from their directions, and their lengths must scale with radius. Samples stacked across the middle of isolated trails give a common transverse profile, which is used with a Gaussian-smoothed longitudinal segment along a quadratic approximation to the local arc. The grid spacing limits the change in endpoint displacement within a region to about one pixel, or about 2.4 px at fast rotation, where the spacing reaches its 32 px minimum. Each fit evaluates the template at the candidate's position.

The rotation model assumes a single center in the frame and an approximately uniform angular sweep. The shared template models one stable shape. Compact wobble that the census reads as point-like follows the point path. Large background variations and overlapping trails can still hide faint stars. The dense correlation is about 2–4 × 10¹⁰ multiply-adds on a 4096 × 4096 frame with a large template (several seconds), and rotation mode builds a local template for each candidate that reaches fitting. Next to a very bright star, residuals of a few percent of template mismatch could leave peaks along its path; such peaks must pass the fit-quality, signal-to-noise and separation tests, and none has been seen on the test frames.

docs.title: fayde
docs.text:
Fayde astrometric plate solver.

Open a :class:Solver once (catalogue and pattern indexes), then call :meth:Solver.solve, :meth:Solver.verify or :meth:Solver.refit per frame. Each returns the report fayde solve, fayde verify or fayde refit prints, as a dict.

Conventions:

  • Input x, y are 0-based (NumPy / Astropy) unless origin=1 (FITS).
  • Report pixel fields (pairs[].x, predicted_x, covariance.crpix_fits, wcs_cards) are FITS 1-based, as in the command-line report.
  • Angles are degrees, the scale arcsec/px, the deadline seconds.

Options (keyword arguments), the same as the command line's:

width, height, ra, dec, radius, pointing_sigma, scale, scale_sigma (fraction), roll, roll_sigma, roll_max, parity ("negative"/"positive"), trail_length, trail_angle, epoch (Julian year), deadline, max_hypotheses, max_sip_order, pixel_error, accept_log_odds, no_priors, no_pointing, no_header_wcs, search_outside_pointing, relax_priors_on_failure, header, instrument, origin.

header is a dict, a list of 80-character cards, or an astropy.io.fits.Header. instrument is a profile dict or the path of a profile JSON file.

docs.title: Solver
docs.text:
A UCAC4 catalogue and pattern indexes, opened once and reused.

ucac4 is the UCAC4 directory (holding u4b/, optionally u4i/); by default the FAYDE_UCAC4 environment variable. indexes are the .fidx files used by :meth:solve. Thread-safe: the GIL is released while solving.

docs.title: solve(x, y, **options)
docs.text: Solve a source list. Returns the report; report["solved"] says whether it solved (an abstention has reason, best_log_odds, hypotheses_tested, search).

docs.title: solve_detection(detection, **options)
docs.text: Solve the sources of a :func:detect report: their 1-based positions, fluxes, errors, star probabilities and truncation, and the stars' trail when the report found one (unless trail_length and trail_angle are given). Takes :meth:solve's options; pass the image's header for its priors.

docs.title: solve_image(image, **options)
docs.text: Find the stars in an image and solve: image is a FITS path, a 2-D array or an Astropy HDU. The image's header gives the priors unless header is passed. Takes :meth:solve's options and :func:detect's; the report adds detection.

docs.title: verify(x, y, wcs, **options)
docs.text: Check a WCS (dict, cards or astropy Header) against the catalogue, unchanged.

docs.title: refit(x, y, wcs, **options)
docs.text: Re-fit a WCS against the catalogue.

docs.title: stars_at(wcs, x=None, y=None, *, ra=None, dec=None, sigma_px=None, sigma_arcsec=None, **options)
docs.text:
Is there a catalogue star here? For pixel positions x, y and/or sky positions ra, dec (degrees) under wcs, the nearest catalogue stars at the epoch, with separation, combined 1σ, p_consistent (Rayleigh tail: chance of this offset or more if the position is the star), p_chance (chance that some star lies this close to an arbitrary position) and consistent.

Options: epoch, header (for the epoch), pixel_error (default pixel 1σ), wcs_sigma_arcsec, search_radius_arcsec (default 30), max_stars (default 3), origin. Positions come back in input order, pixels first.

docs.title: detect(image, **options)
docs.text:
Find stars in an image: a FITS path, a 2-D array (row 0 = FITS row 1) or an Astropy HDU.

Options: fwhm (px; default measured), detect_threshold (σ of a peak, at least 1.5; default: the level that lets one noise peak through per frame, about 5), saturation and gain (default: the header's SATURATE, GAIN/EGAIN), max_sources (default 2000), trail_angle (degrees from +x towards +y: the expected direction of star trails, to choose among directions), no_trails (measure every star as a point, even when the stars are trails), header (dict or cards, for an array), instrument or instrument_path (a profile whose periodic_pattern is subtracted and whose charge_transfer is taken out of the positions; its other fields are not used here) and epoch (Julian year, when the header has no observation time). Returns the report fayde detect prints: settings, background, noise, mode ("points", "trails", "kernel", or "refused") with census, trail, and kernel, sources (the stars, with FITS 1-based x, y, sigma_px, flux, p_star and class), streaks (ends, angle, width, flux) and rejected (hot pixels, cosmic-ray hits, anything on a streak, point-like objects in a trailed frame).

To solve the sources, pass the report to :meth:Solver.solve_detection; its positions are 1-based, which :meth:Solver.solve takes only with origin=1.

docs.title: Fayde plate solver: literature review
docs.text:
Companion to docs/design/plate-solver.md (the "design doc"; section numbers like §5.3 refer to it, and "entry 3.1" to this survey's own entries). Fayde's design: pair seeds when a pointing and a tight scale are given, a 5-ratio pattern hash otherwise, across indexes for different field widths, astrometry.net-style log-odds verification, a weighted TAN+SIP fit, and UCAC4 or Tycho-2.

Sources were found by web search, then papers, abstracts and project pages were read. Each entry says how much was read: [full], the full text or the relevant sections of it; [abstract], the abstract or publisher summary only; [secondary], known only through citing papers, surveys or indexes. In sections 1 to 6, most entries give the citation with this marker, then the idea, the evidence and a paragraph starting "Verdict:", in that order.

Most IEEE/AIAA papers are paywalled and were assessed at abstract level. Verdicts assume the regime Fayde is built for: about 1° FOV, about 3″/px, 30–60 sources, many false detections, stars often trailed, and usually a pointing prior.

Already covered by the design doc and not repeated here: Lang et al. 2010 (astrometry.net: geometric hashing with quads plus Bayesian verification), tetra3 (ESA's rewrite of Tetra, Brown & Stubis 2017: 4-star edge-ratio hash), cedar-solve (a uniform-database fork of tetra3).
