docs.title: 1. Star identification / lost-in-space (star-tracker literature)
docs.text: Star-tracker algorithms are tuned for wide FOVs (8–20°), bright stars, tiny onboard catalogs and no prior. Fayde's hinted path is different: it has a pointing prior, an often tight scale prior, sometimes a roll prior, and a narrow field crowded with false detections. What carries over is mostly about robustness to false stars, and the main lesson is simple: the fewer true stars a hypothesis needs, the more robust the matcher.

docs.title: 1.1 Pyramid and the k-vector
docs.text:
Mortari, Samaan, Bruccoleri & Junkins, "The Pyramid star identification technique", Navigation 51(3), 2004. Mortari, "Search-less algorithm for star pattern recognition", J. Astronautical Sci. 45(2), 1997 (Springer). Mortari & Neta, "k-vector range searching techniques", AAS 00-128, 2000. [secondary] (described consistently in Leake et al. 2020 and in surveys; originals not read.)

The k-vector is a precomputed index over the sorted angular distances of all catalog star pairs. A range query ("every pair with separation in [d−ε, d+ε]") then costs O(1) plus the number of results, with no comparisons. Pyramid takes image star triples, looks each edge up in the k-vector, intersects the candidate sets to identify a triangle, then confirms it with a fourth "pyramid" star. A triangle that the fourth star cannot confirm is rejected, which is how false stars get discarded.

Pyramid is widely called the nominal lost-in-space algorithm. In a six-algorithm comparison (cited in the search results; not read in full) Pyramid had the highest average accuracy with false stars and was the fastest. Its known weakness is a need for accurate focal length (Leake et al. 2020). Fayde's scale prior covers that. The winner of the ESA Kelvins star-ID challenge ("Super k-ID") was built on k-vector techniques (results, [full]).

Verdict: ADOPT the idea, not the algorithm (§5.3). In hinted mode, build a sorted pair list (a k-vector) of the catalog stars inside the hint cone, at query time. That is a few hundred stars and about 10⁵ pairs, built in well under a millisecond. Then seed hypotheses from image star pairs. With a scale prior and known parity, two stars fix a full similarity transform. See entry 3.1 for why 2-star seeds beat 4-star patterns when many sources are false. Fayde tries the pair seeds before its pattern hash (§5.2a).

docs.title: 1.2 Grid algorithm, and its Bayesian and polar variants
docs.text:
Padgett & Kreutz-Delgado, "A grid algorithm for autonomous star identification", IEEE TAES 33(1), 1997. Clouse & Padgett, "Small field-of-view star identification using Bayesian decision theory", IEEE TAES 36(3), 773–783, 2000 (doi:10.1109/7.869495). Lee et al. 2007 (polar grid). [abstract]

The grid algorithm rotates the field so that a pivot star's nearest neighbor lies on the x-axis, rasterizes the neighbors onto a coarse grid, and compares bit patterns. Clouse & Padgett add a Bayesian, adaptive acceptance threshold aimed at a 2° FOV.

Clouse & Padgett report 96.0% correct with <0.3% false positives at 0.5 px noise and 0.8 mag noise. Grid methods depend on the axis-defining neighbor being real and detected, which false or missing stars break. Houtz & Frueh (entry 2.1) say this explicitly for images of trailed stars.

Verdict: SKIP as a matcher. CONSIDER Clouse & Padgett only as further support for likelihood-ratio acceptance with magnitude information (entry 3.7), which Fayde does not use (§5.4).

docs.title: 1.3 Geometric voting
docs.text:
Kolomenkin, Pollak, Shimshoni & Lindenbaum, "Geometric voting algorithm for star trackers", IEEE TAES 44(2), 441–456, 2008, doi:10.1109/TAES.2008.4560198. [abstract]

Every catalog pair whose angular distance matches an image pair votes for both identities. Each image star takes the identity with the most votes, and a second voting round checks the result. The method uses geometry only and draws on the whole image rather than a chosen subset.

The authors report robustness to non-star objects. The LOST open-source tracker (docs) notes "no statistical guarantees" on the wrong-answer rate.

Verdict: CONSIDER as a hinted fallback (§5.3). Inside a hint cone with a tight scale prior, pair voting is cheap and degrades gracefully when the brightest sources are false. Fayde has no voting stage (§5.3); its log-odds test, with the hypothesis-count correction, would gate the votes.

docs.title: 1.4 Liebe triangle
docs.text:
Liebe, "Pattern recognition of star constellations for spacecraft applications", IEEE AES Magazine 8(1), 31–39, 1993, doi:10.1109/62.180383. [secondary]

A star plus its two nearest neighbors gives a triangle feature (two distances and an angle).

The ICPRAM 2023 related-work section and others describe it as fast, but it "suffered limitations with the introduction of false stars". A single false nearest neighbor breaks it.

Verdict: SKIP.

docs.title: 1.5 SP-Search and recursive mode
docs.text:
Samaan, Mortari & Junkins, "Recursive mode star identification algorithms", IEEE TAES 41(4), 2005. [secondary]

Given the previous attitude, recursive mode predicts which catalog stars fall in the FOV and matches them locally, with no pattern search.

Verdict: §5.6 sequence mode is a narrower form: one WCS predicted from a solved neighbor, tried last, when the search finds nothing.

docs.title: 1.6 Multi-Poles Algorithm (MPA)
docs.text:
Schiattarella, Spiller & Curti, "A novel star identification technique robust to high presence of false objects: the Multi-Poles Algorithm", Adv. Space Res. 59(8), 2133–2147, 2017. Schiattarella, Spiller & Curti, "Star identification robust to angular rates and false objects with rolling shutter compensation", Acta Astronautica, 2020 (preprint, [full] for the 2020 paper, which summarizes the 2017 one).

Several "pole" stars are each tried as the center of a pair-distance pattern, in three phases: acceptance, verification, confirmation.

The authors report 100% success with up to 185 false objects against 33 cataloged stars, falling to 66% at 486 false objects against 31 stars (stable attitude). MPA came second in the ESA Kelvins challenge. The ESA-contest version's main improvement was magnitude filtering, which made the confirmation phase unnecessary.

Verdict: CONSIDER, as evidence. The magnitude-filtering result is independent support for a photometric term in the verifier (entry 3.7). The algorithm itself adds nothing beyond 1.1 and 1.3.

docs.title: 1.7 Non-dimensional star-ID
docs.text:
Leake, Arnas & Mortari, "Non-dimensional star-identification", Sensors 20(9):2697, 2020 (arXiv:2003.13736). [abstract]

The method uses dihedral angles of spherical star triangles, which do not depend on focal length, so identification survives a miscalibrated focal length or optical axis.

Verdict: SKIP. Fayde estimates scale itself, and its 5-ratio edge patterns are already scale-invariant (edges over the longest).

docs.title: 1.8 Reverse attitude statistics
docs.text:
Dong, Wang, Wang & Wang, "Reverse attitude statistics based star map identification method", arXiv:2410.23758, 2024 (submitted to IEEE Sensors J.) (arXiv). [abstract]

The method builds candidate attitudes from many matched pairs (with spatial-hash indexing), then takes the mode of the attitude distribution. Matching and attitude solving happen together. It is aimed at missing stars, false stars and star trailing in near-space conditions.

The authors claim a >14.3% better identification rate and >28.5% faster solving than the best existing methods, with field and on-orbit tests. The baselines were not visible in the abstract.

Verdict: CONSIDER, as the same family as 1.3: attitude-space voting. If Fayde implements the hinted fallback, voting in the (roll, offset) space of 2-star seeds is the natural form.

docs.title: 1.9 Surveys and benchmarks
docs.text:
Spratling & Mortari, "A survey on star identification algorithms", Algorithms 2(1), 2009. Rijlaarsdam, Yous, Byrne, Oddenino, Furano & Moloney, "A survey of lost-in-space star identification algorithms since 2009", Sensors 20(9):2579, 2020 ([abstract]; the MDPI and PMC full text was blocked to automated fetch). Toloei et al., "A comparative analysis of star identification algorithms", Astrophys. Space Sci., 2020 (Springer, [abstract]). ESA Kelvins "Star Trackers: First Contact" (2016–2017) (data, results, [full]).

Rijlaarsdam et al. find that published comparisons "can lead to inconsistent conclusions" and give considerations for simulation-based evaluation. Kelvins is the only shared public benchmark found: 10,000 scenes, 10° FOV, 1920×1440, up to 80 false artifacts per scene, centroid noise under 1 px, magnitude noise, Hipparcos. Its final accuracy scores, out of a perfect 9921, are Super k-ID 9708, MPA 9703, "Tetra" (the original hash-table approach behind tetra3) 9672, then others from 9605 down. So a hash-table matcher is within about 0.4% of the best on a false-star-heavy benchmark.

Verdict: CONSIDER. The Kelvins scenes are synthetic, public and false-star heavy, which suits a reproducible regression test of the pattern-hash and seed matchers. LOST (GitHub) implements Pyramid, geometric voting and tetra-style matchers, an independent baseline.

docs.title: 2. Matching trailed stars
docs.text: The literature is thin. No paper found does blind or hinted plate solving of trailed stars with per-source covariance, endpoints and a time-dependent WCS together. The published SSA pipelines mostly either stack the frame so stars become static or feed trail centroids to astrometry.net. For each straight star trail, Fayde's solver receives a center and the larger of its two position errors (streak-detection §7); its input has no trail endpoints, per-source covariance matrix or time term. The useful contributions are narrower.

docs.title: 2.1 Houtz & Frueh: streak detection and plate solving
docs.text:
Houtz & Frueh, "Efficient streak detection and plate-solving techniques", Proc. 8th European Conf. on Space Debris, ESA SDO, 2021 (PDF, [full]).

Streaks are detected with cumulative-sum line integration. For plate solving, only streaks whose length and orientation match the frame's most common values are kept as stars. A polar-grid pattern is built around the brightest star, with the second-brightest streak as the axis, using spherical-triangle radii and angles. It is matched by rotational correlation against catalog patterns, centered on Tycho-2 stars near the a-priori pointing. All stars are then identified from the radius/angle residuals, and QUEST gives the attitude at mid-exposure.

On 15 frames from the POGS 35 cm telescope, on average 11.7 trailed stars were identified per frame, with star-vector errors under 1″. The sample is small and has no false-solve statistics.

Verdict: ADOPT the idea, not the matcher. This is the closest published analog to Fayde's case. It confirms that (a) trail length and direction consistency is the strongest star/non-star cue (Fayde's detector uses it: the census and the trail-against-point comparison set p_star, streak-detection §4.1 and §4.4), and (b) a hinted, pointing-centered search is the practical approach. One step further, not built: in target-tracking mode the common star trail is the sky's apparent motion relative to the tracked target, projected onto the detector. Given the commanded tracking rate and the exposure time, the trail's direction could constrain roll and its length the pixel scale. This is an inference of this survey, not a published method.

docs.title: 2.2 Sease et al.: attitude and rate from streak endpoints
docs.text:
Sease, Koglin & Flewelling, "Long integration star tracker image processing for combined attitude–attitude rate estimation", Proc. SPIE 8739, 2013, doi:10.1117/12.2020004 (UCF record). [abstract], plus a catalog-free follow-up and a UCF thesis (core.ac.uk, [secondary]).

The method treats streak endpoints as corner features. It groups the endpoints into "start" and "end" sets using a cross-product test of the rotation sense, then runs ordinary star-ID and attitude determination on each set. Two attitudes from one image give the attitude rate.

In Monte Carlo runs, endpoint accuracy is better than 0.1 px when more than 20° from the rotation axis, for streaks up to 40% of the FOV. The thesis reports rates within 2% in simulation.

Verdict: CONSIDER. A joint fit of the mid-exposure WCS plus pointing and roll rates would be the least-squares generalization of this: one fit, with covariances, instead of two independent solves. Fayde fits a static WCS (§5.5). Note the asymmetry: endpoint error along the trail is usually much larger than across it (entry 2.4), so endpoint covariances must be anisotropic.

docs.title: 2.3 AURORAS: time-dependent astrometric calibration
docs.text:
Krantz, Bloch, Serda, Flechtner & McMahon-Crabtree, "AURORAS: orbit determination with just one look", AMOS 2025 (PDF, [full], relevant sections).

Event-camera or fast-frame data are shift-stacked so the stars become static and can be plate solved against Gaia. Then a "dynamic astrometric calibration" fits an (x, y, t) → (RA, Dec, t) transform. Residuals before the time-dependent fit show offsets and curvature from the moving tangent plane plus mount jitter; after it they are flat.

The paper shows qualitative residual plots and gives no numbers on astrometric accuracy.

Verdict: CONSIDER a time-dependent WCS, with an optional quadratic time term (pointing acceleration) for non-linear trails, as in long exposures tracking fast LEO targets. Fayde fits a static WCS (§5.5); curved star paths are handled in detection (streak-detection §8).

docs.title: 2.4 Trail fitting for astrometry (producer side)
docs.text:
Vereš, Jedicke, Denneau, Wainscoat, Holman & Lin, "Improved asteroid astrometry and photometry with trail fitting", PASP 124, 1197, 2012 (arXiv:1209.6106). [abstract]

A trail is modeled as a Gaussian PSF convolved with a line segment, and its center, length, angle and flux are fitted.

The fit gives about 3× better astrometry and up to 2 mag better photometry than PSF or aperture methods for trails longer than about 10 px (Pan-STARRS1).

Verdict: ADOPT the trail-model fit. Fayde's detector measures a shared trail length, angle and width, fits each trail with them held fixed, and reports errors along and across it (streak-detection §4.3). The solver takes one isotropic error per source (§6.3); errors that are narrow across the trail and wide along it, and endpoints, would need a change to the input contract and the verifier.

docs.title: 2.5 Rolling-shutter streaks
docs.text:
Schiattarella et al. 2020 (entry 1.6), [full]. Curti et al. (rate estimation from streaks up to 10–25°/s; Sapienza, [abstract]).

A rolling shutter distorts streak length by about 25% (Curti et al.). A first-order compensation gives reliable identification up to 5°/s.

Verdict: SKIP. The frames this survey targets come from global-shutter sensors.

docs.title: 2.6 Astrometry24.NET
docs.text:
Sybilska et al., "Astrometry24.NET – precise astrometry for SST and NEO", Proc. 1st NEO and Debris Detection Conf., ESA, 2019 (PDF, [full] for the introduction and architecture).

Astrometry24.NET is a commercial cloud service that fits streak profiles and solves frames tracked at non-sidereal rates. The paper describes the architecture and accuracy campaigns but gives little detail on the matching algorithm.

Verdict: SKIP. Nothing to port. It could serve as an external accuracy cross-check if real frames were ever run through it.

docs.title: 3. Verification, false-match probability and robust sampling
3.1 The minimal-sample argument (RANSAC)
docs.text:
Fischler & Bolles, "Random sample consensus", Comm. ACM 24(6), 1981. [secondary; standard result]

If a fraction w of sources are real catalog stars, a hypothesis built from k sources is all-true with probability about wᵏ. At w = 0.5, a 4-star pattern (tetra3 or astrometry.net) succeeds 6.3% of the time, a 2-star seed 25%, and a 1-star seed 50%. At w = 0.3 the figures are 0.8%, 9% and 30%. For a source list of 30–60 entries with many false detections, this ratio matters more than any detail of hash design.

Verdict: ADOPT (§5.3). When priors fix scale (and parity), the hinted path should seed from 2-star pairs (entry 1.1). Single-star seeds, when roll is also known, would be the next step: each image–catalog pairing proposes a translation, and the translations vote (not built). The pattern hash remains the blind and weak-prior path.

docs.title: 3.2 PROSAC
docs.text:
Chum & Matas, "Matching with PROSAC – progressive sample consensus", CVPR 2005, doi:10.1109/CVPR.2005.221 (PDF). [abstract], plus reviews.

PROSAC samples hypotheses from a progressively growing set of the top-ranked correspondences rather than uniformly, which is still correct in the limit. The gain depends entirely on how well the ranking predicts correctness.

It needs up to more than 100× fewer samples than RANSAC on CV benchmarks (in one example, 9 samples against about 10⁵), and gives no advantage when the ordering is random.

Verdict: ADOPT (§5.3, §6.3). tetra3/cedar's brightest-first, breadth-first enumeration is already a PROSAC-like ordering, but it ranks by brightness alone. Fayde ranks by p_star × flux (§5.0), and its detector's p_star carries the trail consistency, which predicts "real star" much better than flux alone (the brightest sources in SSA frames are often the target, cosmic rays or blends). Fayde feeds all matchers in that order (p_star × input-order rank when there is no flux). The ordering must be deterministic (requirement 6).

docs.title: 3.3 LO-RANSAC (local optimization)
docs.text:
Chum, Matas & Kittler, "Locally optimized RANSAC", DAGM 2003, LNCS 2781. [secondary; standard]

When a hypothesis looks promising, LO-RANSAC refits the model on its inliers (and iterates) before scoring it. Minimal-sample models are noisy, so scoring the raw model underestimates support.

Verdict: ADOPT (§5.4/§5.5). This matters most for trailed stars and for 2-star seeds. A similarity transform from two stars, ignoring trail rate and distortion, can leave a true match just below threshold. Fayde's flow (§5.4):

  1. A cheap pre-filter.
  2. If it passes, a weighted refit on its matches (similarity → TAN).
  3. Re-match, then compute the log-odds on the refined model.

astrometry.net does a version of this ("tweak" during verification).

docs.title: 3.4 MAGSAC / MAGSAC++
docs.text:
Barath, Matas & Noskova, "MAGSAC: marginalizing sample consensus", CVPR 2019; Barath, Noskova, Ivashechkin & Matas, "MAGSAC++, a fast, reliable and accurate robust estimator", CVPR 2020 (arXiv:1912.05909). [abstract]

MAGSAC removes the hard inlier threshold by marginalizing the model score over the noise scale σ, up to a loose upper bound. MAGSAC++ fits with weighted least squares (IRLS) in place of a hard inlier set.

Verdict: SKIP the algorithm. Fayde has per-source position errors, so the log-odds already uses an explicit noise model, which is what MAGSAC approximates when one is missing. The underlying idea is built: producers' errors are often miscalibrated, so Fayde fits a single global error-scale factor s (covariance × s²) and reports it (§5.5), so a detector that under-reports its errors is visible. It has no prior on s and does not marginalize over it.

docs.title: 3.5 A contrario / number of false alarms (NFA)
docs.text:
The a-contrario detection framework (Desolneux, Moisan & Morel; Abergel & Moisan on trajectories). [secondary] No paper was found that applies NFA to star identification.

A detection is accepted when (number of tests) × P(an event at least this good under the null hypothesis) < ε. The threshold is calibrated against the search size, not set per hypothesis.

Verdict: done (§5.4). astrometry.net's 10⁹ odds is a fixed per-hypothesis threshold. Blind solves test many more hypotheses than hinted ones, so the family-wise false-accept rate differs between them. Fayde counts the hypotheses tested, reports NFA = n_tested × exp(−log_odds) next to the log-odds, and in every search mode compares log_odds − ln(n_tested) with the log-odds threshold, ln(10⁹) by default. This also gives a calling pipeline a single number to record.

docs.title: 3.6 Mixture-model fitting
docs.text:
Hogg, Bovy & Lang, "Data analysis recipes: fitting a model to data", arXiv:1008.4686, 2010. [secondary; well-known]

Each data point is modeled as a mixture: inlier (Gaussian with its covariance) or outlier (broad background). The mixture is fitted or marginalized in place of hard clipping at kσ.

Verdict: ADOPT (§5.4/§5.5). This is the same likelihood the astrometry.net verifier uses (a Gaussian match against a uniform distractor). Fayde's final fit uses it too, as IRLS on the mixture weights with per-source outlier priors from p_star; the local refit before scoring still re-matches within shrinking radii. One noise model, used consistently, is easier to reason about and gives better-calibrated covariances.

docs.title: 3.7 Photometric consistency in verification
docs.text:
Clouse & Padgett (1.2) use 0.8 mag noise inside a Bayesian decision. The MPA authors (1.6) found magnitude filtering was the main improvement for their contest entry. A brightness-referenced method (Sensors 2014, [abstract]) reports speed gains from brightness ordering.

Verdict: CONSIDER (not built: the verifier does not compare brightnesses, §5.4). The literature and this regime suggest the following:

  • Fit the zero point robustly.
  • Use a heavy-tailed (Student-t) magnitude residual, because UCAC4 magm against an unfiltered or wide band, trail photometry, saturation and blends all produce outliers.
  • Weight the magnitude term well below the positional term until it has been calibrated on a corpus of real frames.

The magnitude term is a second discriminator, not a primary one.

docs.title: 4.1 Wahba's problem: QUEST, ESOQ, SVD
docs.text:
Shuster & Oh, "Three-axis attitude determination from vector observations", J. Guid. Control 4(1), 1981 (QUEST). Mortari, "ESOQ: a closed-form solution to the Wahba problem", J. Astronaut. Sci. 45(2), 1997. Markley & Mortari, "Quaternion attitude estimation using vector observations", J. Astronaut. Sci. 48(2–3), 359, 2000, doi:10.1007/BF03546284 (preprint, under the title "New developments in quaternion estimation from vector observations": NTRS). [abstract] Umeyama, "Least-squares estimation of transformation parameters between two point patterns", IEEE TPAMI 13(4), 1991. [secondary; standard]

Davenport's q-method and SVD are the most robust; QUEST, ESOQ and ESOQ2 are faster and adequate for star sensors. Robustness only matters when measurement accuracies differ widely (Markley & Mortari).

Verdict: SKIP QUEST/ESOQ and SVD. At 30–60 stars, speed is irrelevant, and none of these solvers handles anisotropic weights. Fayde's pair seeds use the closed-form two-point similarity in the tangent plane (entry 3.1), once for each allowed parity; pattern seeds fit a similarity to all four stars. The one that verifies is kept. The weighted TAN least-squares fit follows, with one weight per matched pair.

docs.title: 4.2 Distortion representation: SIP vs TPV vs Zernike
docs.text:
Shupe et al., "The SIP convention for representing distortion in FITS image headers", ASP Conf. Ser. 347, 2005. Calabretta & Greisen, "Representations of celestial coordinates in FITS", A&A 395, 2002 (TPV is a registered convention, not part of the standard). Bertin, "Automatic astrometric and photometric calibration with SCAMP", ASP Conf. Ser. 351, 2006. Shupe et al., SPIE 2012 (sip2pv/pv2sip conversion). [secondary], from survey pipeline papers (PTF, SAGES).

SIP (pixel-space polynomials) and TPV (polynomials in intermediate world coordinates) are interconvertible to good precision. SCAMP writes TPV, and pipelines routinely convert it to SIP because most tools read SIP. Zernike is useful only for wide-field optics with a circular pupil, and has no FITS convention.

Verdict: keep SIP; SKIP TPV and Zernike (§5.5, "Won't" confirmed).

docs.title: 4.3 Persistent instrument distortion with per-exposure terms
docs.text:
Bernstein et al., "Astrometric calibration and performance of the Dark Energy Camera", PASP 129:074503, 2017 (arXiv:1703.01679, [abstract]). SCAMP (Bertin 2006), which fits distortion across many exposures at once.

The astrometric model is split into a persistent instrument component (optics, detector), fitted once from many exposures, and a per-exposure component, kept low-order. DECam reaches 3–6 mas per exposure this way.

Verdict: CONSIDER. With 30–60 stars per frame, many of them trailed with large along-trail errors, a per-frame SIP order 3 (14 free coefficients on top of 6 linear ones) is at serious risk of overfitting. A persistent SIP fitted across solved frames could live in the instrument profile, leaving each frame only the linear terms and a low-order correction. Fayde fits SIP per frame and guards the order with held-out cells (§5.5); its profile holds no distortion.

docs.title: 4.4 Model selection and covariance
docs.text:
These are standard statistical results. The F-test assumes nested models with Gaussian, correctly scaled errors. With miscalibrated covariances it over-selects. BIC penalizes parameters by log N. Leave-one-out cross-validation on the matched stars is cheap at N ≤ 60 and robust to error-scale problems.

Verdict: ADOPT (§5.5). Choose the SIP order by BIC and check it on held-out cells (Fayde's rule, §5.5). Report the covariance scaled by the fitted s² (entry 3.4), with s alongside, as Fayde does. Include the catalog position error at the epoch in W (the design already does this), so the covariance is not optimistic when UCAC4 dominates the error.

docs.title: 5.1 HEALPix uniformization
docs.text:
Górski et al., "HEALPix", ApJ 622, 2005. Lang et al. 2010 (uniformize-catalog).

Verdict: keep (§5.2). Nothing better found.

docs.title: 5.2 Fibonacci lattice and spherical-spiral catalogs
docs.text:
González, "Measurement of areas on a sphere using Fibonacci and latitude–longitude lattices", Math. Geosci. 42, 2010 (arXiv:0912.4540, [abstract]). Bauer, "Distribution of points on a sphere with application to star catalogs", J. Guid. Control Dyn. 23(1), 2000 ([secondary]; the spherical spiral method). Variants: charged particles, k-means clustering (GWKM: Somayehee, Nikkhah & Roshanian 2019, J. Navig. 72(4), 948, doi:10.1017/S0373463318001029, [abstract]).

Fibonacci lattices give near-equal-area cells for any point count, with at least 40% lower RMS error in area estimates than latitude–longitude grids. Spherical-spiral catalogs are the star-tracker standard for uniform onboard catalogs.

Verdict: keep (§5.2). cedar-solve's Fibonacci lattice fields for pattern generation plus HEALPix for star selection is a sound combination. No change.

docs.title: 5.3 Rigorous epoch propagation
docs.text:
Butkevich & Lindegren, "Rigorous treatment of barycentric stellar motion", A&A 570, A62, 2014 (arXiv:1407.4664, [abstract]). The same formulae appear in the Gaia DR3 documentation.

The paper gives closed-form propagation of all six astrometric parameters between epochs, reversible, with a full covariance transformation.

Verdict: ADOPT as the reference (§5.1). With UCAC4 (no parallax or radial velocity) the equations reduce to the zero-parallax case, which Fayde's file-backed catalogs use. Fayde grows each axis's position error with the proper-motion error, with no covariance transformation, and the result feeds the fit weights in §5.5.

docs.title: 5.4 UCAC4 error budget and epoch policy
docs.text:
Zacharias et al., "The fourth US Naval Observatory CCD Astrograph Catalog (UCAC4)", AJ 145:44, 2013 (arXiv:1212.6182). [abstract]

Formal position errors are 15–100 mas at the mean epoch, plus 10–20 mas systematic. Proper-motion systematics are about 1–4 mas/yr; random errors are larger for faint stars. Propagated to 2026 (about 26 yr from 2000, somewhat less from UCAC4's central epochs), typical position errors are therefore about 0.05–0.3″. At 3″/px that is 0.02–0.1 px: irrelevant for matching and small for the fit. Gaia DR3 is about 100× better and would only matter for accuracy claims finer than about 0.1 px.

Verdict: ADOPT a two-level policy (§5.1, §5.2).

  1. Build the index at a fixed epoch (for example 2025.0). For 99.9% or more of stars, |µ| < 100 mas/yr, so ±10 yr moves them less than 1″ (0.3 px), well within the pattern tolerance.
  2. Exclude high proper-motion stars from the index (Fayde's cut is about 180 mas/yr per degree of field, §5.2). Query-time catalog reads still see them.
  3. Propagate at query time, to the mid-exposure epoch, for verification and fitting.

Rebuilding the index for each campaign is then unnecessary. Gaia DR3 matters only for accuracy requirements finer than about 0.1 px.

docs.title: 5.5 Aberration for spacecraft observers
docs.text:
Klioner, "A practical relativistic model for microarcsecond astrometry in space", AJ 125, 2003. [secondary] SOFA/ERFA iauAb/eraAb (fully relativistic to about 1 µas). Gravity Probe B context: orbital aberration about ±5.2″, annual about ±20.5″ (via search, [secondary]).

For a telescope in low Earth orbit, β = |v_annual + v_orbital|/c is at most about 1.25×10⁻⁴ (computed for this survey). That shifts the field center by up to about 26″. The differential effect across a 1° field is a scale change of order β, at most about 0.2″ at the field edge, about 0.07 px.

Verdict: CONSIDER ERFA's ab formulation (§6.6). At this FOV, aberration affects only CRVAL and the plate scale, so matching and verification can safely ignore it, and observer state would be an output-accuracy input, never a solve-rate input. Fayde takes no observer state and applies no aberration.

docs.title: 5.6 Index compression
docs.text: No result was found that improves on cedar-solve's layout (a 16-bit key check plus the longest edge in each slot; Fayde stores the edge as f32) for Fayde's scale. Index size is covered in §5.2.

docs.title: 6. Learned / ML star identification
docs.text:
Hepburn-Dickins, Jones, Edwards, Morgan & Bell, "SIGNN – star identification using graph neural networks", WACV 2025 (CVF page, [abstract]). Hepburn-Dickins & Edwards, "Noise robustness of data-driven star classification", ICPRAM 2023 (PDF, [full]). RPNet (Xu et al. 2019), 1-D CNN classifiers (Yang et al. 2022), and Wang et al., Sensors 2021 ([secondary]).

SIGNN is a graph-attention network over a Hipparcos star graph with edges below 3°.

ICPRAM 2023 reports 98.5% accuracy on augmented samples, but 13.5% of stars misidentified on simulated Stellarium images. A 0.999 confidence cut removed 99.85% of wrong identifications but discarded 39% of correct ones. There is no head-to-head comparison against Pyramid or tetra3. Most learned methods are trained for wide-FOV Hipparcos star trackers. None addresses trailed stars, sub-degree FOVs with UCAC4 density, or calibrated false-accept rates.

Verdict: SKIP. Not credible for production where a wrong WCS is worse than no WCS. Fayde's correctness rests on a likelihood-ratio verifier with a hypothesis-count correction, which ML methods do not provide. If anything, a learned source classifier belongs on the producer side, feeding p_star, which the contract already supports.

docs.title: 7. Source and streak detection (2026-11-16)
docs.text: Survey for detection in frames with point-like stars (docs/design/detection.md). Reference implementations were read at the head of their default branches; [full], [abstract] and [secondary] as above, [code] for source code.

None of them measures the star width and adapts the filter to it, reports a per-star position error to the matcher, models cosmic rays or hot pixels other than by minimum area or sharpness, finds the center of a saturated star with a bleed trail, or traces streaks before solving (astrometry.net removes sources in over-dense rows and columns only).

docs.title: 7.2 Centroid accuracy
docs.text:
• Cramér–Rao bound, Gaussian star: √2·σ / SNR per axis background-limited (0.60 FWHM / SNR), σ / √N source-limited (King 1983 [full]; Mendez, Silva & Lobos 2013 [full]; Mortensen et al. 2010 [full], whose eq. 6 gives (16/9)·σ²/N + 8π·σ⁴·b/N² for a Gaussian-weighted centroid).
  • A matched filter followed by a 3 × 3 quadratic fit reaches the bound for FWHM 2.8 to 5.6 px at SNR 5 to 100; a fixed kernel does not at the extremes; a 7 × 7 center of light is several times worse (Vakili & Hogg 2016 [full]).
  • A parabola through three samples of a Gaussian peak is biased toward the pixel center; the same fit on the logarithms has no bias (Naidu & Fisher 1991 [full]).
  • Undersampled stars (σ 0.66 px): moment methods have pixel-phase floors of 0.02 to 0.04 px; only a pixel-integrated profile fit goes lower (Fialho 2025, arXiv:2507.17560 [full], preprint).

Verdict: ADOPT the matched filter with a log-quadratic 3 × 3 fit; derive the error per source.

docs.title: 7.3 Statistics of noise peaks
docs.text:
• Height distribution and density of local maxima of smoothed Gaussian noise: Cheng & Schwartzman 2015, 2017, 2018 [full]; Bond & Efstathiou 1987 [full]. For a Gaussian kernel of σ = s, maxima above u per unit area tend to u·exp(−u²/2) / (2^{5/2}·π^{3/2}·s²), the figure LSST uses for false-peak counts (DMTN-006 [full]).
  • On pixels, with a kernel of about 1 px, the continuous formula is 25 to 35% conservative (Lin, Schwartzman & Davenport 2025, arXiv:2501.13239 [full], preprint).
  • False discovery rate for astronomical sources: Miller et al. 2001 [full], Hopkins et al. 2002 [full] (pixel-level); local rate: Efron 2008 [full]. No published use of the peak-height test for optical star detection was found (it is used on CMB and radio maps).

Verdict: ADOPT the peak density as a threshold and null model, bounded by the pixel count.

docs.title: 7.4 Streaks
docs.text:
Method Cost Reaches Note Fast Radon transform (Nir, Zackay & Ofek 2018 [full]) 0.9 s per megapixel 0.1 × the pixel noise for a long streak Stars must be removed first; GPL-3 Median Radon (Stark et al. 2022 [full]), Fourier-slice Radon (Hickson 2018 [full]) 3 to 10 s per megapixel 0.13 to 0.4 × the pixel noise Canny + Hough (acstools.satdet [code]); kernel-based Hough (Rubin maskStreaks, DMTN-197 [full]) 4 to 22 s per image the per-pixel detection threshold Needs long streaks Blobs, moments and a line fit (ZTF, PTF [full]; ASTRiDE [code]) 0.6 to 25 s per image 1 to 3σ per pixel Many false candidates Grouping point detections into lines (Rubin FindGlintTrails [code]; Storkey et al. 2004 [full]) milliseconds detected fragments Hessian line points (Steger 1998 [secondary]; Lowe 2004 [full] for the curvature ratio) per pixel per-pixel contrast The local test Fayde uses at peaks Neural networks (DeepStreaks, MaxiMask, ASTA [abstract]) 1 to 25 s per frame on a CPU Outside a few ms per megapixel

Steger 1998 links Hessian line points into lines, and in trailed frames Houtz & Frueh 2021 (entry 2.1) and Sharma et al. 2023 (entry 8.4) detect trails before plate solving. For frames with point-like stars, no surveyed plate solver traces streaks before solving.

Verdict: ADOPT ridge-like peaks as seeds and trace from them (Fayde's own tracer); SKIP Radon and Hough (cost; they find streaks too faint to disturb the star list).

docs.title: 8. Trailed stars and faint streaks (2026-11-17)
docs.text: Survey for one detector that handles trailed stars, streaks and faint streaks (docs/design/streak-detection.md). Sources already in entries 2 and 7.4 are not repeated. Many publisher PDFs could not be read; each entry says what was. Figures marked derived were worked out during the survey and are not from a source.

docs.title: 8.1 The frame's common trail
docs.text:
Source Idea Numbers Verdict Danescu & Turcu 2026, Sensors 26(5), 1628, doi:10.3390/s26051628 [full] LoG filter, top 5% of pixels, connected components, second moments; components with eccentricity over 0.65 vote; the frame's trail is the median direction and median major-axis length; template = 1 px line ⊛ Gaussian astrometry.net solved 39 of 40 frames after filtering with the template, 15 of 40 before; under 1 s for 1536 × 1024; fails when trails reach about 12% of the frame width ADOPT: cheap, deterministic, the median ignores a satellite or cosmic rays Lévesque 2011, AMOS poster [abstract] Track-rate frames: trail direction from the Radon transform of the Fourier modulus; length next; an iterative matched filter; star trails measured before satellites are sought none obtained CONSIDER as the segmentation-free check Li, Zhang, Yao & Sun 2013, Opt. Precision Eng. 21(10), 2656, doi:10.3788/OPE.20132110.2656 [abstract] Direction from PCA of the binarized cepstrum; length from the minima of the spectrum's Radon profile along it 0.14° and 0.27 px on natural images CONSIDER for refining long trails Cannon 1976, IEEE TASSP 24(1), 58; Moghaddam & Jamzad 2007, EURASIP JASP 068985; Oliveira, Figueiredo & Bioucas-Dias 2014, IEEE TIP 23(1), 466 [abstract] Blur kernel from the cepstrum or the Radon transform of the spectrum natural images only SKIP as primary: noise-sensitive, not tested on star fields Sun, Xing, You & Wei 2013, Opt. Express 21, 20096 [abstract]; Hou et al. 2021, Math. Probl. Eng. 8819277 [abstract] Star-tracker smear direction and length from image derivatives, bispectrum or the spectrum's Radon profile not obtained CONSIDER

Derived: the power spectrum of a field of identical trails is |PSF̂|²·sinc² times a speckle factor from the star positions, so in an ideal frame the sinc's zeros survive any star layout. Cropping, noise and trails that vary across the frame fill them in. For trails under about 2 FWHM the first zero falls where the PSF has already removed the power: the spectrum can only help with long trails.

docs.text:

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
Versioning rules: docs/versioning.md.

Versions up to 0.2.1 were development versions and were not published; their notes are kept because the index files and their hashes date from 0.1.0.

• Periodic background patterns. An instrument profile's periodic_pattern field lists the frequencies of stripes from readout pickup; Fayde fits their amplitude and phase in 32 × 32 pixel tiles and subtracts them before detection. fayde calibrate --periodic-pattern finds the frequencies from the frames' power spectra. The detection report gains periodic_pattern. On 193 real frames from one camera, whose stripes hold about 18% of the background variance, frames tracking satellites solved 77 of 84 (66 without) and frames whose stars are points 109 of 109, as before.
  • Charge-transfer smear. An instrument profile's charge_transfer field takes the CCD's smear out of the positions Fayde detects: traps displace faint stars away from the readout, more the farther they are from it. fayde calibrate --charge-transfer --ucac4 DIR fits it from solved frames (the readout axis and edge too), with its growth per year when five or more dated frames span a year. It applies to --image, fayde detect --instrument and Python detect/solve_image; source lists given with --sources are left as they are. The detection report gains charge_transfer (null without a term) and, per star, charge_transfer_px. On 175 solved real frames from one camera (not in the repository), the offset between faint and bright stars at the top rows fell from 0.29 to 0.04 px, the error scale of frames whose stars are points from 1.52 to 1.32, and no frame stopped solving.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Trailed stars from an image. When every star is a straight trail of one length and direction (the telescope tracked a satellite or slewed), fayde detect, --image and fayde.detect/solve_image measure the stars as trails. A trail census decides points, trails or refused from two independent estimates and a regional check, an aimed filter finds the trails, and one fit per trail gives its position with errors along and across it. Trails shorter than 7 FWHM are left to the point detector. On 109 real frames whose stars are points the star lists are unchanged; on 84 real frames tracking satellites, 66 solve (9 before). Design and measurements: docs/design/streak-detection.md.
  • The detection report gives mode, census, trail, sigma_along_px and sigma_across_px. The tracked object comes out as class point, and fayde solve --image passes the measured trail to the solver.
  • --trail-angle (Python detect(trail_angle=)) chooses among trail directions. fayde detect -o writes the trail into the source list (TRAILLEN, TRAILANG), and fayde solve --sources reads it back.
  • Stars smeared along a curved path are detected with an empirical template, and field rotation with templates that vary across the image. The detection report adds kernel mode and a kernel field with the template's dimensions, star count, path length, bend and region count.
  • A frame measured in trails or kernel mode that gives no solution before reaching the time and hypothesis limits is solved again with its stars measured as points (fayde solve --image, Python solve_image). The report's retried_as_points says so, and describes the first attempt if the retry ends in an error.
  • --no-trails (fayde detect, fayde solve; Python no_trails) measures every star as a point, skipping the trail census.
  • The trail census holds up against cosmic rays and background structure. On frames crowded with radiation hits, it masks sharp charge deposits and keeps narrow tracks out of the direction vote. On those frames, and when the first census finds no trail among bright elongated sources, a second census takes anchors from bright sources after a finer local background and any strong periodic pattern are removed. On 30 simulated trailed frames with 80–1,000 hits per cm² per second, or a smooth background field of 5–20 ADU on 5 ADU noise, the census finds trails on all 30, with the direction within 0.09°.
  • On frames whose stars all trail, radiation hits don't set the stars' width. When the round peaks are as narrow as hits, and the elongated peaks along the frame's trail direction are more than twice as wide, detection takes the trails' width across the trail. Hits are flagged by comparing their sharpness with that width: on simulated track-rate frames, 120 of 120. A hit isn't reported as a tracked object, the tracked object is reported at its position with its flux, and roughly collinear trails aren't traced as a satellite streak, whose light is even along its length.
  • Solver.solve_detection(report) in Python solves a fayde.detect report directly. Its positions are FITS 1-based, which Solver.solve takes only with origin=1; passing them without it moved the solution by a pixel.
  • FAYDE_UCAC4 names the catalog directory when --ucac4 is left out, and for fayde.Solver() with no directory.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • fayde calibrate takes each frame's header pointing at the centre of the image it solved, using the image's size when the header does not give it, as image and source-list solves have done since 0.3.2.

• Header coordinates whose last field reads exactly 60, such as RA = '20:29:60.0' (59.96 s rounded up by the writer), are read as the next minute instead of being rejected; an RA of exactly 24 hours is 0. Before, such a frame lost its header pointing and, without an index, was not searched at all: 80 of 46,219 frames in a real archive. A decimal RA or DEC written with padding, such as RA = ' 12.5', is read as degrees; before, the padding made it read as hours.
  • Distortion is fitted only where the stars support it. A SIP order is kept only if no lower order predicts held-out cells of the frame as well. When the hint has a scale or roll, a solution with distortion is fitted again as TAN with its scale and roll free; a TAN outside the hint's limits that fits the sources at least as well means no solution, and one inside them is kept if its posterior odds are higher. Before, a hint whose scale was wrong by more than its limits, or matches with errors in one region, could give a solution bent by up to 146 px in the corners.
  • Image and source-list solves use the WCS position of the delivered frame centre, including for cropped images. --header and fayde calibrate read the metadata of image extensions. North-pole TAN headers use the FITS default orientation. Eighth- and ninth-order SIP solutions write inverse polynomials that Fayde can read back.
  • Streak photometry masks bright stars that cross a streak. The report marks affected streaks with photometry_masked; their flux includes an estimate for the covered ridge, and their SNR uses only unmasked samples. For Rust users, fayde_detect::Streak gains the field photometry_masked.
  • Distortion tune-ups honour the hypothesis cap, an expired pair-seed search stops before reading the catalogue, and relaxed-prior timings include both attempts. Legacy indexes keep their verified file hash in the solution provenance. fayde verify ignores the request's priors, as documented.
  • -o may not name any input: fayde detect refuses its --image, and fayde calibrate its --solved list and every frame and WCS the list names. fayde calibrate -o writes the profile atomically.
  • A detection threshold below 1.5σ is refused: it kept noise peaks with no light, reported as stars with negative flux.
  • When the stars' FWHM is at most one pixel at full resolution, Fayde keeps bright sources that are too sharp for the usual shape checks; hot pixels and compact cosmic-ray hits can then reach the source list. On simulated frames of FWHM 0.45 and 0.6 px, completeness rose from 0.23–0.84 to 0.98–1.00 with purity 0.98–1.00. Source lists for 2 px FWHM frames are unchanged.
  • Detection estimates the sky background of frames that background subtraction clipped at a floor, such as zero, by fitting each tile as a left-censored normal. On a simulated frame with 90% of the sky at the floor, 95 of 579 detections were stars before and 100 of 100 after. On 35 real frames with 25–36% of their pixels at zero, all still solve; the fit residual fell on 31 (median 0.40 to 0.35 px) and solutions moved by at most 0.14″. Constant padding alone leaves the standard background estimate in use.
  • The stars' width is no longer taken from a crowd of cosmic-ray hits: in the histogram of sizes, a mode at least three quarters as tall as the tallest counts as the stars' when it is the widest, dip or not.
  • A warning when no observation time is found (catalogue positions at J2000.0). The IMAGEW/IMAGEH cards of wcs_cards are whole 80-character cards, so the cards join into a header.
  • Python: an image passed with header=None uses the header of its HDU, and arrays are converted to 32-bit floats once instead of through a 64-bit copy.
  • Comments that restated the code are removed from the source, scripts and workflows.
  • All 109 real point-source frames of the test set solve with 0.3.1 and with 0.3.2.

• pip install fayde also installs the fayde command. It runs the same code as the release binary (fayde-cli is now a library as well, with fayde_cli::run), so a solve finds the same solution either way; only the timings in the report differ.
  • Solving is faster, with the same results to the last bit. Measured on 109 real frames, one thread: a solve with a pointing and a scale takes 6.0 ms on average, from 22.5 ms; with a pattern index and a pointing, 2.3 ms from 18.8 ms; with no priors, 1.9 ms from 3.7 ms.
  • The catalogue stars of a pointing prior are read as hypotheses need them. Only the brightest stars of the prior's cone are read for seeding; the fainter ones are read around each hypothesis that passes the pre-filter. A 2° prior around a 0.6° frame is 46 frame areas, and reading all of it was most of a solve. A consequence: a missing zone file is an error when a seed or a hypothesis needs it, no longer whenever it lies inside the prior.
  • The UCAC4 cone search works out each star's direction once, not three times, and decides the cone from it; the exact separation is computed only for a star at the cone's edge.
  • The pair-seed table is sorted only where a lookup reaches it; sources are matched to reference stars on a grid of cells; a fit projects each star from its unit vector.
  • A pointing known better than its hard limit is searched close in first. When the pointing's 1σ (--pointing-sigma, or the instrument profile) is at most a sixth of the limit, pair seeds look within 3σ of the pointing and widen to the limit only when that finds nothing. Measured on 146 real source lists: 8.7 ms per list at a 2° limit, 1.1 ms at 0.25°. With the default σ (a quarter of the limit) nothing changes.
  • fayde calibrate writes an instrument profile from frames Fayde has solved: scale, parity, the roll rule for a header keyword, and the pointing's 1σ. A profile needs no other solver: solve some frames with their header pointing and a nominal --scale, then calibrate.
  • Instrument profiles can carry pointing_sigma_deg, pointing_radius_deg (the hard limit, in place of --radius) and header_wcs (false: do not read the pointing or scale from a WCS in the header).
  • --no-header-wcs (Python: no_header_wcs=True) reads the pointing from RA/DEC or OBJCTRA/OBJCTDEC only, for headers whose WCS may be another solver's solution.
  • fayde compare builds its requests as fayde solve does and takes --instrument, --no-header-wcs and --hinted-only. It reports how far apart Fayde's solutions with priors and blind are; another solver's WCS in the frame file is a second opinion.
  • A UCAC4 copy without u4i/u4index.unf is searched by RA in each zone file, which is in RA order, instead of read whole: a solve that took 350 ms takes 6 ms, as with the index. Keep u4hpm.dat, which holds the proper motions of the fastest stars.
  • New in the library: Catalog::cone_brightest (the n brightest stars of a cone; a catalogue can override it to rank by magnitude before working out positions), brightest_first, Ucac4Catalog::cone_hits_ra_search, TanWcs::vector_to_pixel, Wcs::vector_to_pixel, TangentPlane, KdTree::any_within, Header::without_wcs, calibrate_profile and RequestOptions::no_header_wcs.

The first public release: on GitHub, PyPI and crates.io.

  • Giving neither --sources nor --image (or both) is reported before anything else runs, so like every command-line mistake it leaves an existing -o file in place. --help now says which errors come with a JSON report (from the moment the inputs are read) and which are on stderr only.

  • Source lists are Fayde's own format, named for what they are: --sources (and --at-sources) replace --xyls (and --at-xyls), which are still accepted. The file is unchanged in substance, a FITS binary table with X, Y and optional columns, so earlier files still read; by convention it is named after its frame, frame.sources.fits. Lists that Fayde writes are labelled EXTNAME = 'SOURCES', and giving an image where a source list is expected (or the reverse) is reported as such. In the library, read_xylist/write_xylist/ Xylist are read_sources/write_sources/SourceList.

  • Fayde finds the stars itself when given a FITS image instead of a source list: fayde solve|verify|refit --image frame.fits (the image's header is used for the priors unless --header is given), fayde detect --image frame.fits [-o frame.sources.fits], and fayde.detect(...) / Solver.solve_image(...) in Python (a path, a 2-D array or an Astropy HDU). For point sources (sidereal tracking or stare). FITS images of every BITPIX are read (not fpack-compressed ones). Detection options: --fwhm, --detect-threshold, --saturation, --gain, --max-sources; SATURATE and GAIN/EGAIN are read from the header.

  • The detector (crate fayde-detect) is Fayde's own design, docs/design/detection.md. It needs no settings: it measures the stars' width and matches its filter to it (wide stars are binned), and sets its threshold from one noise peak per frame. Each star gets a position, a 1σ position error and a star probability from one closed-form fit at its peak. Hot pixels and cosmic-ray hits are set aside, saturated stars are centred from their clipped region, and streaks are traced and reported with their ends, angle, width and flux; nothing on a streak is handed to the solver. It is built for difficult frames: the star width is the widest distinct size among compact sources (radiation hits can outnumber stars), each peak is tested against a ring around it (stray light), and narrowness is judged against the stars' own narrow axis (frames smeared by a drift). 2 to 7 ms per megapixel on one core, the same bits on every machine. Its work is bounded on hostile input (a width far larger than the frame, a saturation level in the background, a frame saturated all over). The detection report gains classes, streaks, rejected (what was set aside) and, per source, p_star and class; sources is the list handed to the solver.

  • fayde verify no longer touches the path given with -o. It names the option as unused, as before; 0.2.0 and 0.2.1 then went on to delete a file at that path when the check failed or produced no solution.

  • Solved .wcs files name the commit as well as the version in their comment cards.
  • Releases are built by GitHub Actions: the fayde command and Python wheels for Linux, macOS and Windows, every file run on its platform before it is published, with SHA256SUMS.
  • THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.md holds the licences of the Rust crates compiled into binaries and wheels; both carry it.
  • Metadata for crates.io and PyPI. The Fayde crates require exactly their own version of each other, and each carries LICENSE, NOTICE and a README.

• -o: any failed run (an unreadable input, a wrong catalogue directory, a solver error, no solution, a failed write) leaves no file at the output path. An error before the solve used to leave an earlier run's WCS there, where it would pass for this frame's.
  • -o naming one of the run's inputs (--wcs, --xyls, --header, --instrument, --ucac4, an --index) is refused before anything runs. fayde refit --wcs a.wcs -o a.wcs with no solution used to delete the WCS it was given.
  • fayde_core::fsutil is internal (hidden from the documentation, not covered by the versioning rules).

Fixes from a review with hostile inputs. Several change what Fayde does with input it used to accept, so this is a minor release (see the versioning rules). Index bytes and content hashes are unchanged from 0.1.0. On a real 146-frame comparison set the header-prior solve rate and agreement are identical to 0.1.1.

  • No panic on extreme or non-finite WCS and pixel values (fayde verify --at 1e308,1e308, a NaN SIP coefficient): pixel_to_sky is defined for every input, and a non-finite header number is an error naming the keyword.
  • A damaged u4i/u4index.unf is reported as such instead of crashing a cone search.
  • fayde index build checks its parameters and its output path before the catalogue scan. Rejected now: a lattice of more than 1e9 fields (--oversampling 1e12), a non-finite --mag-limit, an epoch outside 1800 to 2200.
  • A closed stdout pipe (fayde solve ... | head -1) ends quietly instead of panicking.
  • CROTA2 (with CDELT, no CD or PC matrix) is applied; such a WCS was read unrotated.
  • Epochs outside 1800 to 2200 are clock errors: from a header (MJD-OBS holding a Julian Date, an unset DATE-OBS) they are skipped with a warning; from --epoch they are an error.
  • -o: the output path is checked before solving, the report is printed before the file is written, a failed write leaves no temporary file, and a run that finds no solution removes a file already at that path instead of leaving an earlier WCS there.
  • Header pointing: coordinates the header declares as FK4 or of another equinox are not used (with a warning); a right ascension out of range is rejected instead of wrapped; the first card of a repeated keyword is used, as in cfitsio and Astropy (it was the last).
  • Options dropped by --no-priors or --no-pointing, and options fayde verify and fayde refit do not use, are named in warnings or on stderr instead of ignored in silence.
  • --max-sip-order above 9 is an error (the SIP convention's limit).
  • Error messages name the file they are about.
  • Temporary files (the -o write check, .wcs and index writes) are created with O_CREAT|O_EXCL under unpredictable names: an existing file or symlink at that name is never followed or truncated, and a failed write removes only the file Fayde created.
  • The example instrument profile is profiles/example.json; the catalogue cross-check reads ucac4_oracle.json.

• Licence: Apache-2.0 (was MIT OR Apache-2.0, provisional). LICENSE, NOTICE and CITATION.cff added; wheels and binary archives carry them.
  • Index set built and its content hashes published (docs/index-set.md): 1.0° 1ddf14fa50ad59dd, 1.3° 4ad74722223054e1. Index bytes unchanged from 0.1.0: the builder identity stored in an index (fayde_index::BUILDER) now changes only when the index-building code does, not with every crate version, so a patch release keeps every hash.
  • Python: py.typed, typed reports (fayde.Report, fayde.AtReport), checked with mypy --strict in CI.
  • fayde solve|verify|refit --help and fayde index build --help list options with defaults.
  • The commit id is recorded in builds from git archive source archives (.git_archival.txt).
  • fayde compare reads headers as fayde solve --header does.
  • Solved .wcs files ask for a citation in their comment cards.
First release: solve, verify (including --at), refit; Python bindings; identical index bytes on macOS, Linux and Windows; Linux binaries and wheels.

docs.title: fayde detect
docs.text:
fayde detect --image <frame.fits> [-o <frame.sources.fits>] [options]

Finds stars in a FITS image as points, straight trails, or stars smeared along curved
paths. Prints a JSON report with the settings, mode (points, trails, kernel, refused),
census, trail or kernel measurements, stars' width, background, noise, and sources with
position (FITS 1-based), error (along and across the trail too), flux, star probability and
class, the streaks traced (ends, angle, width, flux), and what was set aside (hot pixels,
cosmic-ray hits, anything on a streak, point-like objects in a trailed frame). -o also writes
the sources as a source list for --sources, with the trail.
The same detection runs inside `fayde solve|verify|refit --image <frame.fits>`, which also
reads the frame's header from the image unless --header is given.

  --image <frame.fits>        FITS image: BITPIX 8/16/32/64/-32/-64 with BSCALE/BZERO/BLANK,
                              primary HDU or first IMAGE extension (not fpack-compressed)
  --fwhm <px>                 stellar FWHM                     default: measured from the image
  --detect-threshold <sigma>  peak threshold, filtered image   default: one noise peak per
                              frame (about 5 for 4 megapixels)
  --saturation <adu>          saturation level                 default: SATURATE, else the
                              level of flat-topped stars
  --gain <e/adu>              gain, for the stars' own noise   default: GAIN or EGAIN, else none
  --max-sources <n>           brightest sources kept           default 2000
  --trail-angle <deg>         expected direction of star       default: none; the trail used
                              trails, from +x towards +y       is measured from the image
  --no-trails                 measure every star as a point, even when the stars are
                              trails (skips the trail census)
  --instrument <profile.json> subtract the profile's periodic pattern and take its
                              charge-transfer smear out of the positions (its other fields
                              are for the solve)                          default: none
  --epoch <year>              observation year, for a smear    default: the header's
                              that changes with time
  -o <frame.sources.fits>     also write the sources as a source list (Fayde's FITS table:
                              X, Y, FLUX, SIGMA, P_STAR, TRUNCATED); name it after the frame

docs.title: fayde calibrate
docs.text:
fayde calibrate --solved <list> [options] [-o <profile.json>]

Writes an instrument profile (for --instrument) from frames Fayde has solved: the pixel scale,
the parity, the rule that gives the roll from a header keyword, and how far the header's
pointing is from the solved frame centre. Values are medians of the solutions, so a few poor
solutions do not move them; at least 5 solved frames are needed, and more are better.

A profile needs no other solver. Solve some frames with the pointing from their headers and a
nominal scale (fayde solve --scale <arcsec/px> ... -o frame.wcs), then calibrate from those.

  --solved <list>          text file, one solved frame per line: the frame's FITS file (for
                           its header), a tab, the WCS file of its solution; # starts a comment
  --roll-keyword <KEY>     header keyword with the instrument's own roll, degrees: the profile
                           gets the rule roll = offset + sign x KEY       default: no roll rule
  --binning <XKEY>[,<YKEY>]  header keywords of the binning factors: the profile's scale is
                           then the unbinned one                           default: none
  --name <text>            the profile's name
  --no-header-wcs          measure the header pointing from RA/DEC or OBJCTRA/OBJCTDEC, not a
                           WCS in the header, and make the profile tell the solver the same
  --charge-transfer        also fit the CCD's charge-transfer smear (faint stars displaced
                           away from the readout edge): the listed FITS files must be the
                           images; needs --ucac4. Detection options (--fwhm ...) apply
  --periodic-pattern       also find stripes from readout pickup (a wave of fixed frequency in
                           every frame's background), to subtract before detection; the listed
                           FITS files must be the images
  --ucac4 <dir>            UCAC4 directory, for --charge-transfer
  -o <profile.json>        also write the profile to a file

The profile goes to stdout. Its "calibration" member holds the numbers behind it: frames
used, spreads, worst deviations.
